Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
justification: Harmful-success benchmark for coding agents; safety eval, not inference.
hype_justification: Agent-safety benchmark with frontier-model results, topical.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.

title: FedReady: Bounded Agents for Federation Formation
justification: Bounded agents for federated-learning federation formation; not inference serving.
hype_justification: Federated-learning niche.
abstract: Federated learning (FL) runtimes standardize aggregation and deployment, but each new study still requires federation formation: selecting task-eligible sites and preparing their local data and task code for federated training or analysis. This preparation recurs when the target changes, while raw records and site-private mappings are excluded from cross-site FL messages. We present FedReady, a system that performs federation formation with bounded LLM agents. Agents propose shared contracts, local adapters, and task code; the runtime owns workflow state and accepts artifacts only after checks tied to their digests. Candidate site discovery prioritizes recall; local eligibility verification checks task support before site admission. Once participating sites and artifacts are fixed, conventional federated training or analysis proceeds without readiness agents. Across 39 simulated retinal sites and four tasks, discovery reaches recall 1.00 at precision 0.65; local eligibility verification removes all 17 false positives without losing an eligible site-task pair. The participating sites supply 45,575 task-record instances and complete four 100-round jobs, including one with a runtime-generated contract. Across ten patient cohorts, preparation supports seven patient populations and holds endpoints at three sources as unsupported. Comparison with manually prepared reference populations and analysis (the manual reference) gives a maximum survival-curve difference of 0.001133. We also analyze 19 development failures, targeted classification ablations, and standalone and heterogeneous agent configurations. These results establish the feasibility of task-specific data preparation before ordinary FL training or analysis.

title: A Scaling Theory of Multi-Epoch Pretraining: Late-Time Overfitting and Ensembling
justification: Scaling theory for multi-epoch pretraining and ensembling; training-side.
hype_justification: Scaling-laws theory draws interest; data-bound regime is topical.
abstract: In the near future language model pretraining will become bound by total data rather than total compute. Such a regime requires revisiting scaling laws and scaling law theory. Motivated by prior works that have found utility in ensembling, we study how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly shape generalization when training data are fixed. In language-model experiments on FineWeb, logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration, delays optimal stopping, and can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a common training horizon. To analyze this interaction between data reuse and ensembling, we derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles, tracking error correlations across epochs and models. Ensembling reduces the prediction variance responsible for late-time growth in expected test error, changing the optimal stopping time. We use these stopping times to derive compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model sizes. Under this allocation, ensemble size grows with compute at least as fast as training time per member, while excess test loss above the limiting loss decreases as a power of compute.

title: DynaSolver: A Neural Operator for Autoregressive 4D Flow Prediction with Dynamic Boundaries
justification: Neural operator for 4D CFD with moving boundaries; unrelated.
hype_justification: SciML/robotics niche.
abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD), but most are designed for static geometries and are not equipped to model unsteady flows induced by continuously moving boundaries. We study dynamic-boundary 4D CFD prediction for articulated moving geometries and introduce RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved robotic CFD benchmark spanning diverse morphologies and flow conditions. To address the computational and autoregressive challenges of this setting, we propose DynaSolver, a neural operator that explicitly conditions on boundary evolution and causal flow history. DynaSolver employs an efficient physical-token formulation that amortizes point-to-token projection across the operator stack, substantially reducing repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining accurate point-level reconstruction. We further introduce Replay-Augmented Parallel Training, which exposes the model to autoregressively generated histories while preserving parallel dense supervision, narrowing the gap between ground-truth-conditioned training and autoregressive rollout. Experiments on RoboCFD-4D show that DynaSolver achieves the best full-rollout accuracy among a broad range of learned CFD surrogates, with its advantage increasing as rollout proceeds, indicating substantially reduced autoregressive error accumulation. Project page: https://made-gpt.github.io/DynaSolver-ProjectPage.

title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
justification: Agentic physiological glucose control; medical application.
hype_justification: Novel medical-agent benchmark, some cross-interest via Claude results.
abstract: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.

title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
justification: Tracing LLM discovery capacity to training-data monofacts; training analysis.
hype_justification: Discovery-from-training-data question is intriguing, strong author list.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.

title: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents
justification: Meta-agent evolving reasoning/inference strategies (prompting procedures), not serving systems.
hype_justification: 'Evolving inference strategies' with cost savings is catchy and practical.
abstract: A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint,executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs.74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does.

title: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models
justification: VLM zero-shot reward models for robotics; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Robotics-RL niche with prompt-based appeal.
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video's internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks---matching or surpassing post-trained reward models---and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.

title: Not All Reasoning Generalizes: A Case Study on Learning Generalizable Reasoning Strategies in RLVR
justification: RLVR reasoning generalization study; training/RL analysis.
hype_justification: RLVR generalization is trending among RL-reasoning researchers.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can enable generalizable improvement for large language model (LLM) reasoning. This paper studies how to incentivize such generalization via reasoning strategies. We study this question with a controllable equation-solving framework: finding multiple inputs x for equations f(x)=y, where f is a non-bijective string function. This setting makes reasoning strategies observable while supporting a clear definition of easy-to-hard out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, e.g., more solutions, longer y, etc. We uncover a subtle RLVR failure: it teaches the model to solve in-distribution tasks with high accuracy and structured step-by-step derivation, yet under OOD shifts, the same model abandons derivation and collapses to ineffective brute-force enumeration, causing sharp accuracy drops. This observation reveals the deeper challenges of RLVR generalization as it is neither incapable base model nor reward hacking, since the model succeeds in-distribution with the correct reasoning strategy. The key to mitigating this failure is an indirect intervention that surprisingly helps: co-training with bijective inversion tasks. Although these bijective tasks are actually not uniformly harder and even further from the non-bijective OOD evaluation, they make derivation more certain and substantially restore the correct strategy and accuracy under OOD shifts. This effect further motivates our theoretical analysis: outcome-only RLVR can shape reasoning processes through implicitly crediting the effective reasoning strategies more, even without process supervision. To conclude, our analysis framework and findings systematically reveal the crucial role and incentivization of reasoning strategies in RLVR generalization under OOD shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/ziqipang/rl_meta_thinking.

title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
justification: Muon vs AdamW optimizer fine-tuning gap; training optimization.
hype_justification: Muon is a hot optimizer topic; surprising reversal result will draw clicks.
abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon's advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token-parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training.

title: From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
justification: Neuro-symbolic solver for Zebra puzzles; reasoning, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Niche neuro-symbolic logic work.
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generation has substantially improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, including code generation, data analysis, and exam-style question answering. Despite these advances, purely neural LLMs continue to struggle with elementary logical reasoning problems and lack the determinism, soundness, and reliability characteristic of symbolic reasoning systems. Conversely, classical symbolic methods such as SAT solving and exact cover guarantee correctness and completeness, but require problems to be expressed in highly specialized formal encodings, limiting their applicability to natural language inputs. In this work, we present a synergistic neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by combining neural semantic parsing with deterministic exact cover reasoning. Given a Zebra-style logic puzzle in natural language, an LLM translates entities and constraints into structured tool calls that construct an exact cover instance. A symbolic solver then computes the solution and provides feedback to iteratively refine invalid, under- or overconstrained encodings, exploiting the uniqueness property of Zebra puzzles. We conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple parameter scales, post-training paradigms, and LLM families. The results demonstrate that our hybrid approach consistently outperforms strong plain neural baselines, including CoT prompting, as well as recent neuro-symbolic methods.

title: Subspace Node Pruning
justification: Node pruning to cut inference time, tested on OPT/LLaMA-2; inference-oriented compression but general.
hype_justification: Solid pruning method matching LLM-Surgeon, moderate adoption potential.
abstract: Node pruning is the art of removing computational units such as neurons, filters, attention heads, or even entire layers to significantly reduce inference time while retaining network performance. In this work, we show that a broad family of importance measures, from activation-based to Fisher-based, share a common quadratic form. Through a lower-triangular change of basis, this form yields a pruning subspace in which entire nodes can be removed while the impact of the lost units is simultaneously recovered via linear least squares. Furthermore, the importance measures within our subspace are decoupled and additive through an orthogonalization of the layer activations, allowing multi-node pruning within layers without interference between importance scores. Our method, Subspace Node Pruning (SNP), outperforms the compared baselines on VGG-16 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet. On OPT-125M and LLaMA-2 7B, SNP matches the state-of-the-art LLM Surgeon at a 40-shot schedule and outperforms it whenever fewer shots are used, all without any retraining after pruning.

title: Semantic Self-Consistency: Enhancing Language Model Reasoning via Semantic Weighting
justification: Semantic self-consistency for reasoning aggregation; prompting technique.
hype_justification: Incremental self-consistency variant.
abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have rapidly improved their performance on a broad number of tasks, they still often fall short on reasoning tasks. As LLMs become more integrated in diverse real-world tasks, advancing their reasoning capabilities is crucial to their effectiveness in nuanced, complex problems. Wang et al.'s self-consistency framework reveals that sampling multiple rationales before taking a majority vote reliably improves model performance across various closed-answer reasoning tasks. Standard methods based on this framework aggregate the final decisions of these rationales but fail to utilize the semantic information detailed in the step-by-step reasoning paths. Our work introduces semantic self-consistency, enhancing this approach by incorporating and analyzing both the reasoning paths of these rationales in addition to their final decisions before taking a majority vote. These methods not only improve the reliability of reasoning paths but also cause more robust performance on complex reasoning tasks.

title: Towards Optimal Multi-draft Speculative Decoding
justification: Optimal multi-draft speculative decoding via optimal transport; core LLM inference acceleration.
hype_justification: Speculative decoding is a hot inference topic; theoretical bounds are citable.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become an indispensable part of natural language processing tasks. However, autoregressive sampling has become an efficiency bottleneck. Multi-Draft Speculative Decoding (MDSD) is a recent approach where, when generating each token, a small draft model generates multiple drafts, and the target LLM verifies them in parallel, ensuring that the final output conforms to the target model distribution. The two main design choices in MDSD are the draft sampling method and the verification algorithm. For a fixed draft sampling method, the optimal acceptance rate is a solution to an optimal transport problem, but the complexity of this problem makes it difficult to solve for the optimal acceptance rate and measure the gap between existing verification algorithms and the theoretical upper bound. This paper discusses the dual of the optimal transport problem, providing a way to efficiently compute the optimal acceptance rate. For the first time, we measure the theoretical upper bound of MDSD efficiency for vocabulary sizes in the thousands and quantify the gap between existing verification algorithms and this bound. We also compare different draft sampling methods based on their optimal acceptance rates. Our results show that the draft sampling method strongly influences the optimal acceptance rate, with sampling without replacement outperforming sampling with replacement. Additionally, existing verification algorithms do not reach the theoretical upper bound for both without replacement and with replacement sampling. Our findings suggest that carefully designed draft sampling methods can potentially improve the optimal acceptance rate and enable the development of verification algorithms that closely match the theoretical upper bound.

title: Eco-MobiLLM: Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning on the Mobile Device via Server Assisted Side-Tuning
justification: Server-assisted on-device LLM fine-tuning; training/comms, not inference.
hype_justification: Mobile fine-tuning niche.
abstract: There is a huge gap between numerous intriguing applications fostered by on-device large language model (LLM) fine-tuning (FT) from fresh mobile data and the limited resources of a mobile device. While existing server-assisted methods (e.g., split learning or side-tuning) may enable LLM FT on the local mobile device, they suffer from heavy communication burdens of activation transmissions. In addition, their multiple on-device forward passes over the same samples across training epochs lead to substantial iterative computation on the mobile device. To address those issues, we develop Eco-MobiLLM, an efficient LLM FT method which can be deployed on the mobile device via server-assisted side-tuning. To reduce communication cost, Eco-MobiLLM develops an activation shortcut that transmits only the tokens involved in the loss calculation instead of full activation matrices to guide the side network tuning. Besides, to improve computing efficiency and further accelerate FT convergence, Eco-MobiLLM introduces a novel two-stage training paradigm, which allows the server to reuse historical activations and saves the mobile device from repeatedly computing forward passes for the recurring data samples. Extensive experimental results demonstrate Eco-MobiLLM's superiority.

title: Beyond Isolated Dots: Benchmarking Structured Table Construction as Deep Knowledge Extraction
justification: Structured-table extraction benchmark over long documents; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Long-context extraction benchmark, moderate interest.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to extract and synthesize structured information from complex real-world documents, yet they typically produce unstructured, hard-to-verify paragraph-style outputs. We introduce AOE (Arranged and Organized Extraction), a bilingual benchmark that evaluates LLMs' ability to distill long-form, multi-document inputs (64k to 1.8M tokens) into structured tables. AOE comprises 12 tasks across four domains (academic, financial, legal, and medical), each grounded in genuine analytical needs, with schema guidance provided to isolate extraction quality from formatting variance. We evaluate 12 frontier LLMs (both open-weight and proprietary) under four generation settings of increasing autonomy: direct full-document input, RAG-based retrieval, offline document-browsing agent, and online web-search agent. Even the best-performing model achieves only 42.7% Cell F1, and retrieval-augmented approaches often degrade rather than improve performance, revealing that structured extraction from long contexts remains a fundamental challenge - an "Area of Effect" (AOE) that impacts all tested systems.

title: Efficient Collaborative LLM Fine-Tuning over Heterogeneous Mobile Devices via Many Backbones to One Side-Network Tuning
justification: Collaborative federated LLM fine-tuning over mobile devices; training-side.
hype_justification: Federated fine-tuning niche.
abstract: Collaboratively fine-tuning (FT) large language models (LLMs) over heterogeneous mobile devices fosters immense potential applications of personalized intelligence. However, such a vision faces critical system challenges. Existing federated LLM fine-tuning approaches remain limited by prohibitive on-device resource overhead, straggler-prone synchronous aggregation, and the assumption of a unified pretrained backbone across heterogeneous devices. In this paper, we propose EC-MobiLLM, a novel design for efficient collaborative LLM fine-tuning across heterogeneous mobile devices and heterogeneous backbones. EC-MobiLLM adopts a server-assisted side-tuning paradigm to minimize on-device overhead and pioneers non-blocking asynchronous collaboration to accelerate training. Moreover, EC-MobiLLM introduces adaptive feature alignment to support collaboration across heterogeneous backbones, aligning with practical needs in real-world deployments. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that EC-MobiLLM can maintain robust fine-tuning performance while achieving extremely low on-device memory, with at least 95.2\% reduction in computation overhead, 93.2\% reduction in communication costs and $5.1\times$ faster convergence compared to existing methods, validating its efficacy for practical LLM adaptation over heterogeneous mobile devices.

title: A Financial Brain Scan of the LLM
justification: Sparse-autoencoder interpretability for finance LLMs; not inference systems.
hype_justification: SAE interpretability is trendy; finance angle broadens appeal slightly.
abstract: We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to "brain scan" large language models, mapping internal activations to interpretable concepts and enabling targeted "steering" of specific features. We show that prompting models to adopt specific preferences activates many unintended concepts, complicating causal inference. In contrast, SAEs permit smooth, more isolated steering of target concepts. Furthermore, our scans reveal a stark disconnect between the model's internal feature contributions and its self-generated explanations, showing that these explanations are unreliable guides to its reasoning. Finally, SAEs provide a lightweight intervention for existing models, producing interpretable embeddings and allowing researchers to attenuate specific economic biases.

title: PersonaFuse: A Situation-Aware Post-Training Framework for Adaptive LLM Behavior in Enterprise Tasks
justification: Situation-aware post-training for enterprise behavior; training/alignment.
hype_justification: Enterprise persona-adaptation niche.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in enterprise settings to support task execution and workflow automation. Despite the strong performance of general-purpose models on standard benchmarks, organizations often need to adapt them to domain-specific tasks and operational constraints in practice. However, existing post-training approaches introduce capability trade-offs and lack mechanisms for situational adaptation. In this work, we propose PersonaFuse, a post-training framework that enables situation-aware behavioral adaptation in LLMs. Grounded in Trait Activation Theory and operationalized through the Five-Factor Model, PersonaFuse dynamically adjusts model behavior based on task context using a mixture-of-experts architecture with trait-level experts and a context-aware routing mechanism. We evaluate PersonaFuse at three levels. At the capability level, it achieves balanced improvements across general reasoning, interaction quality, and safety without introducing trade-offs. At the workflow level, it improves task completion in enterprise scenarios involving tool use and structured execution across both B2B and B2C tasks. At the deployment level, we analyze model selection under cost and safety constraints using a capability-cost frontier framework, showing that models adapted with PersonaFuse achieve more favorable trade-offs and are consistently selected as optimal across deployment scenarios. PersonaFuse provides a practical framework for developing LLMs that are not only capable, but also adaptable and deployable in real-world enterprise environments.

title: SLogic: Subgraph-Informed Logical Rule Learning for Knowledge Graph Completion
justification: Subgraph-informed logical rules for knowledge-graph completion; unrelated.
hype_justification: KGC niche.
abstract: Logical rule-based methods offer an interpretable approach to knowledge graph completion (KGC) by capturing compositional relationships in the form of human-readable inference rules. While existing logical rule-based methods learn rule confidence scores, they typically assign a global weight to each rule schema, applied uniformly across the graph. This is a significant limitation, as a rule's importance often varies depending on the specific query instance. To address this, we introduce SLogic (Subgraph-Informed Logical Rule learning), a novel framework that assigns query-dependent scores to logical rules. The core of SLogic is a context-aware scoring function. This framework is in line with the specificity principle in commonsense reasoning. This function determines the importance of a rule by analyzing the subgraph locally defined by the query's head entity, thereby enabling a differentiated weighting of rules specific to their local query contexts. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that SLogic achieves competitive performance among rule-based methods. It also generates query-dependent, human-readable logical rules that serve as explicit explanations for its inferences.

title: Free Draft-and-Verification: Toward Lossless Parallel Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models
justification: Training-free lossless parallel decoding for diffusion LLMs; directly inference acceleration.
hype_justification: dLLM parallel decoding is trending; lossless speedup claim is attractive.
abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as a compelling paradigm for language modeling, offering the unique potential for highly efficient inference via multi-token parallel decoding. However, unlocking this potential remains challenging. High-quality generation typically defaults to one-token-per-step static decoding, while existing parallel algorithms rely on heuristic confidence thresholds, introducing a fragile trade-off between decoding efficiency and generation quality. To overcome this, we introduce Free Draft-and-Verification (FreeDave), a novel training-free and model-free fast decoding algorithm. FreeDave capitalizes on the inherent properties of dLLMs by treating future token predictions as ``free drafts'' and rigorously self-verifying them in subsequent forward passes. Theoretically, FreeDave searches for a shorter decoding path that is guaranteed to reproduce the exact sequence generated by static decoding, achieving algorithmically lossless acceleration. With a sufficiently large draft budget and a verification frontier that does not retreat, it can use the fewest possible model forward passes among feasible paths. Extensive evaluations on math reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that FreeDave can boost the number of generated tokens per model forward (TPF) by up to 5.48$\times$ and tokens per second (TPS) by up to 3.94$\times$, while robustly maintaining generation quality and avoiding the task-specific performance degradation faced by heuristic methods. Code is available at https://github.com/cychomatica/FreeDave.

title: MAGDrop: Momentum Adaptive Gradient Dropout With Provable Generalization Guarantees
justification: Adaptive gradient dropout with PAC-Bayes bounds; training regularization.
hype_justification: Theoretical training method, narrow audience.
abstract: Standard dropout applies a fixed, uniform noise rate to all units, ignoring available gradient information. We propose momentum adaptive gradient dropout (MAGDrop), a Bayesian linear layer that adapts per-unit weight noise by tracking an exponential moving average of gradient magnitudes. Units with large recent gradient magnitudes receive less noise to preserve learned features; units with below-average gradient magnitudes receive more noise to promote exploration. This adaptation transforms the classifier head into a data-dependent Bayesian predictor whose mean predictor has no additional inference cost. Our primary contribution is a certificate-aware low-rank posterior, MAGDrop-Subspace, that addresses the tension between strong accuracy and tight bounds from probably approximately correct (PAC)-Bayes theory. A full-head stochastic posterior incurs a Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence of approximately 8,625 nats. By confining the posterior to an $r$-dimensional subspace constructed from an independent prior-construction sample $S_0$ and certifying on an independent sample $S$ with $S_0\perp S$, MAGDrop-Subspace reduces KL by approximately a factor of 800 while keeping accuracy close to the baseline. On CIFAR-10 with a 13-layer convolutional neural network and $r=50$, MAGDrop-Subspace achieves a PAC-Bayes Gibbs-risk bound of 0.1882 at 90\% confidence using binary KL inversion, compared with 0.4439 for the full-head baseline. Mean-predictor accuracy is 82.31\%, compared with 83.74\% for the baseline. Complementary accuracy experiments on ImageNet-1K show that MAGDrop reaches top-1 accuracy similar to the strong baseline: 78.57\% compared with 78.51\% on the base Vision Transformer with $16\times16$ patches, and 82.14\% compared with 82.23\% on ConvNeXt-Base.

title: Why Freeze the Encoder? A Controlled Study of End-to-End Sequence-Graph Learning for User Behavior
justification: End-to-end sequence-graph user-behavior learning; unrelated to inference.
hype_justification: Behavior-modeling niche.
abstract: Modeling user behavior couples two distinct signals: a per-user sequence of events and a persistent user-to-user relation graph. Standard pipelines preserve these native formats by combining them in two stages: a sequence encoder is pretrained, its per-user embeddings are frozen, and a graph model is trained on top to allow for cheap serving and cross-task reuse. We ask a simple question: does training the sequence and graph models end-to-end help, and if so, when? To isolate the impact of the training strategy, we hold a standard sequence-encoder-to-GNN pipeline fixed and vary only the optimization method; on Brightkite, a matched control that starts both pipelines from the same pretrained encoder and changes only whether it is updated attributes a 10.6-point MRR gain to end-to-end updating. Across relationship prediction and fraud detection on five real-world datasets, we find that the benefit of end-to-end training is conditional: it improves clearly over frozen two-stage pipelines on relationship prediction, where the relation graph appears to carry much of the signal, whereas gains shrink where the predictive signal is largely node-local (fraud detection), a regime in which a text-fed relational graph transformer achieves competitive results. Furthermore, recasting the data as a temporal graph yields inconsistent results compared to this native sequence-graph formulation. Ultimately, this work provides a controlled empirical account of when jointly training the two structures helps.

title: SAMBA: Toward an EEG Foundation Model via Differential Mamba and Coordinate-Driven Spatial Embedding
justification: Mamba EEG foundation model touting efficient inference, but domain-specific.
hype_justification: EEG+Mamba niche despite efficiency framing.
abstract: Modeling long-context electroencephalography (EEG) signals is critical for learning generalizable EEG representations, as EEG recordings are acquired at high sampling rates and often span extended durations that capture evolving neural states beyond short task- specific windows. Transformer-based models have shown promise in modeling short sequences of a few seconds; however, their quadratic complexity limits scalability to longer contexts. Moreover, substantial variability in electrode montages across datasets and recording devices poses a major challenge for building EEG models that generalize across domains. We propose SAMBA, a self-supervised learning framework with a Mamba- based U-shaped encoder-decoder architecture, which effectively captures long-range temporal dependencies and montage variability in EEG data. Leveraging the inherent ability of Mamba in processing long context sizes, we introduce: (1) Temporal Semantic Random Masking for semantic-level sequence reconstruction, (2) a Multi-Head Differential Mamba module to suppress redundancy and emphasize salient temporal structures, and (3) a Coordinate-Driven Spatial Embedding that learns unified embeddings in a three- dimensional Euclidean space, enabling robustness across devices. Experiments on thirteen EEG datasets across diverse tasks, electrode configurations, and sequence durations demonstrate that SAMBA achieves competitive or improved performance compared to recent state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining low memory consumption and efficient inference. The learned spatial weight maps exhibit close alignment with task-relevant neurophysiological regions, highlighting the interpretability of SAMBA. The code is available at: https://github.com/Jiazhen-Hong/SAMBA

title: Structured Prompts Improve Evaluation of Language Models
justification: Structured prompting for LM evaluation (DSPy+HELM); eval methodology.
hype_justification: DSPy/HELM integration may interest eval practitioners.
abstract: As language models (LMs) are increasingly adopted across domains, high-quality benchmarking frameworks are essential for guiding deployment decisions. However, frameworks such as Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) typically evaluate models under a single static prompt configuration, even though model behavior depends strongly on prompt choice. As a result, reported scores can reflect prompt choice as much as model capability. Declarative prompting frameworks, such as DSPy, offer a scalable way to operationalize this evaluation protocol by evaluating models under structured prompting strategies rather than static prompts. Here, we conduct a reproducible DSPy+HELM benchmarking study and quantify how prompt choice impacts benchmark outcomes. Using five prompting methods, we evaluate four frontier and two open-source LMs across seven benchmarks against HELM baseline scores and find that prompt choice can materially impact leaderboards. Structured prompting improves performance (by 6% on average), alters comparisons (leaderboard rankings shift on $5/7$ benchmarks); chain-of-thought provides the strongest cost-performance tradeoff while more advanced optimizers offer smaller additional gains. Beyond the known intuition that prompts affect outputs, our benchmarking study integrates structured prompting into an established evaluation framework and quantifies how prompt choice alone impacts leaderboards. We open-source (i) DSPy+HELM Evaluation (https://github.com/stanford-crfm/helm/pull/3893) and (ii) Prompt Optimization Pipeline (https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/dspy-helm).

title: Multicultural Spyfall: Assessing LLMs through a Dynamic Multilingual Social Deduction Game
justification: Multilingual social-deduction game benchmark; unrelated to inference.
hype_justification: Playful dynamic benchmark, modest attention.
abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has necessitated more robust evaluation methods that go beyond static benchmarks, which are increasingly prone to data saturation and leakage. In this paper, we propose a dynamic benchmarking framework for evaluating multilingual and multicultural capabilities through the social deduction game Spyfall. In our setup, models must engage in strategic dialogue to either identify a secret agent or avoid detection, utilizing culturally relevant locations or local foods. Our results show that our game-based rankings are consistent with Chatbot Arena rankings on the overlapping models. However, we find a significant performance gap in non-English contexts: models are generally less proficient when handling locally specific entities and often struggle with rule-following or strategic integrity in non-English languages. We demonstrate that this game-based approach provides a scalable, leakage-resistant, and culturally nuanced alternative to traditional NLP benchmarks. The dataset (game history) and source code can be accessed here: https://huggingface.co/datasets/haryoaw/cultural-spyfall and https://github.com/haryoa/cultural-spyfall.

title: On the Runway Cascade of Transformers for Language Modeling
justification: Attention-rewiring for causal transformers; architecture/language modeling.
hype_justification: Parameter-free attention tweak, incremental.
abstract: In decoder-only (causal) transformers, the computation graph created by causal masking routes information through both direct-path attention and indirect paths formed by intermediate tokens. We denote these indirect paths between token pairs as their runways. We argue that certain failure modes of causal transformers as observed by a growing body of recent works are likely exacerbated by a misalignment between these two information propagation modes. We formalize runway cascade as a phenomenon whereby this misalignment results in redundancies and irrelevant information cascading to token representations despite adequately learned attention patterns. As a solution, we propose runway-aware rewiring as a more explicit way of incorporating runway context directly into each token's direct-path attention. This mechanism re-wires the attention pattern for each token based on a summary of its runway landscape, enabling awareness of accumulating representational influences and allowing for more balanced information propagation. Our proposed methodology introduces no additional parameters and can seamlessly be integrated into standard attention mechanism. Empirically, our rewired transformer results in steady improvements in general language modeling as well as noticeably stronger information retrieval and extrapolation abilities compared to standard transformers.

title: Dynamic Expert Sharing: Decoupling Memory from Parallelism in Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion LLMs
justification: Dynamic expert sharing decouples memory from parallelism for MoE diffusion LLM inference; cuts activations/latency.
hype_justification: MoE+dLLM serving efficiency is hot; strong practical speedups.
abstract: Among parallel decoding paradigms, diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising candidate that balances generation quality and throughput. However, their integration with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures is constrained by an expert explosion: as the number of tokens generated in parallel increases, the number of distinct experts activated grows nearly linearly. This results in substantial memory traffic that pushes inference into a memory-bound regime, negating the efficiency gains of both MoE and parallel decoding. To address this challenge, we propose Dynamic Expert Sharing (DES), a novel technique that shifts MoE optimization from token-centric pruning and conventional expert skipping methods to sequence-level coreset selection. To maximize expert reuse, DES identifies a compact, high-utility set of experts to satisfy the requirements of an entire parallel decoding block. We introduce two innovative selection strategies: (1) Intra-Sequence Sharing (DES-Seq), which adapts optimal allocation to the sequence level, and (2) Saliency-Aware Voting (DES-Vote), a novel mechanism that allows tokens to collectively elect a coreset based on aggregated router weights. Extensive experiments on MoE dLLMs demonstrate that DES reduces unique expert activations by over 55% and latency by up to 38%, while retaining 99% of vanilla accuracy, effectively decoupling memory overhead from the degree of parallelism.

title: MindGuard: Guardrail Classifiers for Multi-Turn Mental Health Support
justification: Guardrail classifiers for mental-health support; safety, not inference.
hype_justification: Clinical-safety niche with released benchmark.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for mental health support, yet their conversational coherence alone does not ensure clinical appropriateness. Existing general-purpose safeguards often fail to distinguish therapeutic disclosures from genuine clinical crises, and progress on developing better ones is bottlenecked by a lack of clinically grounded evaluation resources. To address this gap, we introduce a risk taxonomy, developed in collaboration with PhD-level clinical psychologists, that identifies actionable harm (self-harm and harm to others) while preserving space for safe, non-crisis therapeutic content. We release MindGuard-testset, a dataset of multi-turn conversations annotated at the turn level by clinical experts, which is, to our knowledge, the first public benchmark with turn-level clinical risk labels for multi-turn mental health support. We also release an automated red-teaming (ART) framework designed to measure how safety classifiers affect downstream model behavior in adversarial multi-turn interactions. Using synthetic dialogues generated via a controlled two-agent setup, we train MindGuard, a family of lightweight safety classifiers (with 4B and 8B parameters). Our classifiers reduce false positives at high-recall operating points and, when paired with clinician language models, help achieve lower attack success and harmful engagement rates compared to general-purpose safeguards. We release all models, training and human evaluation data, and the ART framework.

title: To See or To Please: Uncovering Visual Sycophancy and Split Beliefs in VLMs
justification: Visual sycophancy diagnostics in VLMs; evaluation, not inference.
hype_justification: VLM-failure diagnostics, moderate interest.
abstract: When Vision-Language Models (VLMs) answer correctly, do they rely on the image? We introduce a Tri-Layer Diagnostic Framework that asks three questions of every (image, question) pair when the image is blanked: does the model register that the image is missing (Latent Anomaly Detection, LAD), does its output distribution depend on the image (Visual Necessity Score, VNS), and does it nonetheless commit to a content answer? The cascade assigns each pair of any existing benchmark to one of four modes: Perceptual Blindness, Language Shortcut, Visual Sycophancy (the blank image registers and matters, yet the model commits to a fabricated answer), or Robust Refusal. Across nine open-weight VLMs and 9,000 model-sample pairs, 28.1% are Visual Sycophancy, 18.6% Language Shortcut, 5.6% Perceptual Blindness, and 47.8% Robust Refusal. The modes are strongly model-specific: the Qwen3-VL models refuse on blank input in 93-98% of pairs, whereas Pixtral-12B commits to an answer in 72%. Within-generation scaling increases Visual Sycophancy in both Qwen2.5-VL (7B->72B: 25.5->40.1%) and Llama-3.2-Vision (11B->90B: 34.3->48.0%), while the newer Qwen3-VL generation nearly eliminates it. A blinded human study confirms that LAD and VNS track what annotators observe, and that 80% of Visual-Sycophancy responses carry no textual sign that the image was blank.

title: SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments
justification: Co-evolving agents and learning environments via RL; agent training.
hype_justification: Self-evolving agents is a trending RL theme.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly learn through interaction, yet their training process often evolves unevenly: the policy changes with experience while the learning environment continues to provide largely fixed forms of support. As training progresses, this creates a growing mismatch between what the agent currently struggles with and what its learning process emphasizes. We call this phenomenon Agent-Learning Environment Misalignment (ALEM). We introduce SEAL, a framework for synergistic co-evolution of agents and learning environments. SEAL turns verifier-grounded execution failures into a shared diagnostic signal that coordinates two complementary forms of adaptation: it reshapes the support available in subsequent interactions and adjusts how the policy learns from collected trajectories. In this way, the learning environment follows the agent's evolving failure profile while both sides remain grounded in the same executable feedback. Across three backbones on BFCL V3, SEAL consistently improves over matched Vanilla RL, reaching 40.25% versus 30.75% with Qwen2.5-7B. A matched factorial ablation further yields a +5.00-point interaction estimate for the coupled configuration. The same trained checkpoints also show positive transfer to the evaluated BFCL V4 and $τ^2$-bench domains. These results suggest that coordinating how an agent learns with the environment it learns from is a promising direction for self-evolving tool-use agents.

title: Beyond Augmentation: Score-Guided Pathological Prior for EEG-based Depression Detection
justification: EEG depression detection with score-guided classification; unrelated.
hype_justification: Clinical-EEG niche.
abstract: Deep learning-based Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) detection using Electroencephalography (EEG) is fundamentally constrained by the "small-sample dilemma." Prevailing generative data augmentation methods not only incur heavy computational overhead but also risk introducing synthetic noise, thereby blurring classification boundaries. To challenge the traditional "data quantity first" convention, we propose a novel framework "Beyond Augmentation": Score-Guided Classification (SGC). SGC does not synthesize pseudo-samples; instead, it utilizes an unsupervised generative network architecture to model the structural and statistical anomaly degrees of samples, serving as the core "Pathological Prior". This prior, after robust normalization, is explicitly fused with deep feature representations, thereby precisely guiding the classifier's decision boundary. Furthermore, to dynamically adapt to varying channel configurations, we propose a Cross-Channel Spatial Adaptation module, utilizing a spatial mapping mechanism to effectively resolve the hardware heterogeneity of mismatched channels in multi-center datasets. Extensive experiments on the Mumtaz2016 and high-density MODMA datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and exceptional generalizability of our method under the challenging "zero data augmentation" setting and at "zero sample synthesis cost". Keywords: Electroencephalography (EEG), Depression Detection, Anomaly Score, Diffusion Models, Few-Shot Learning

title: The Price of Partial Information with Switching Costs: A Complete Characterization for Feedback Graphs
justification: Online-learning regret theory with feedback graphs; unrelated.
hype_justification: Learning-theory niche.
abstract: We study how switching costs affect minimax regret under partial feedback. Which features of the feedback preserve the $\sqrt T$ rate, and which force the $T^{2/3}$ rate? We address this question in the framework of feedback graphs, which interpolate between full information and bandits: playing an action reveals the losses of its out-neighbors in a known directed graph. Prior work on feedback graphs with switching costs gave algorithms with regret of order $T^{2/3}$, but matching lower bounds only for restricted classes of graphs, leaving the question open. We establish a complete characterization of the minimax regret with switching costs for all feedback graphs: $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt T)$ if the graph is strongly revealing, meaning that every pair of distinct actions has an endpoint that observes the losses of both; $\widetildeΘ(γ^{1/3}T^{2/3})$ for every other observable graph, where $γ$ is the domination number; and linear otherwise. In particular, tournaments, in which every action observes its own loss and each pair of actions is joined by one directed edge, sit at the phase transition: they behave like full information, but deleting the edge of any pair forces the rate $T^{2/3}$. Hence an action that observes all losses is neither necessary nor sufficient for the rate $\sqrt T$. Our algorithm TournamentSteering for the strongly revealing case rests on a new principle: each observed comparison of two actions serves both to estimate losses and to steer play, and the loss reduction from steering pays for the variance of the estimates. For every strongly revealing graph, distributing the comparisons among observing actions keeps this variance, and hence the regret, polylogarithmic in the number of actions, by an argument similar to the greedy construction of logarithmic dominating sets in tournaments.

title: CVE-Conditioned Exploit Generation with LLMs: A Data-Centric Study of Benchmarking and Fine-Tuning
justification: CVE-conditioned exploit generation; security fine-tuning study.
hype_justification: LLM-for-offensive-security is attention-grabbing but niche.
abstract: We study the task of CVE-conditioned exploit generation, where a model drafts proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits given software vulnerability context. We adopt a data-centric approach, constructing a high-quality dataset via multi-stage preprocessing and introducing a scalable evaluation framework with LLM-as-judge and fine-grained rubrics. Under this unified setup, we benchmark 17 large language models across 8 evaluation criteria, providing systematic insights into their zero-shot capabilities. We further show that a compact 8B open-weight model, when fine-tuned on curated data, achieves over 42.5% improvement in exploit quality and rivals some proprietary models when combined with simple test-time rejection strategies. Our results highlight the importance of data quality, structured supervision, and evaluation design for reliable exploit generation, suggesting that these factors can be as critical as model scale in adapting LLMs to cybersecurity tasks.

title: A Self-Evolving Agent for Longitudinal Personal Health Management
justification: Self-evolving health agent with governed memory; agent memory, not inference.
hype_justification: Medical self-evolving agent, open-sourced, moderate interest.
abstract: Medical large language models and agents show strong single-encounter question answering and evidence interpretation but struggle to accumulate and govern experience across encounters. We present HealthJev, an open-source agent separating shared safety rules and medical knowledge from a private longitudinal memory and distilling lessons from completed cases. To filter out erroneous lessons before they affect future behaviour, we self-train JevGate, a lightweight System-One model that decides which lessons enter memory; each decision takes a median of 86 milliseconds and about 1,000 input tokens, sustaining experience accumulation at negligible run-time overhead. On a longitudinal benchmark of 90-day simulated daily interactions for 20 users built from real MIMIC-IV trajectories, HealthJev outperformed a memory-free ReAct agent and three memory-augmented frameworks, with all paired comparisons significant. Across six tasks spanning clinical records, medical imaging, genomics and clinical text, HealthJev improved every task with a mean gain of 13.3 percentage points over the base condition, surpassing all baselines. The frozen library transferred to six further backbones with macro-average gains of 6.8 to 15.1 percentage points, and one task's library brought gains on other tasks. These results indicate that governed, self-evolving memory supports longitudinal personal health management beyond single encounters. HealthJev is publicly available at https://github.com/HC-Guo/Self-Evolving_HealthJev.

title: Behavioral Residualization for Unsupervised Intrusion Detection in Automotive CAN Networks
justification: Unsupervised CAN-bus intrusion detection; unrelated.
hype_justification: Automotive-security niche.
abstract: Modern vehicles exchange safety-critical messages over the Controller Area Network (CAN), a bus designed for low cost and real-time operation that offers neither authentication nor encryption. Once an attacker reaches the network, arbitrary frames can be injected. Existing detectors frequently rely on surface cues (previously unseen identifiers, constant payload bytes, or irregular DLC values). These cues yield near-perfect scores on public corpora whose attacks are separable by exactly those rules, yet they collapse when the adversary simply reuses legitimate identifiers. We introduce per-ID behavioral residualization (PIRD). Fourteen temporal, protocol and payload statistics are extracted from sliding windows belonging to each arbitration ID and then expressed as standardized residuals relative to that ID's own benign baseline. When the resulting residual vectors are supplied to six standard unsupervised detectors, mean F1 rises in the majority of experimental cells (21 of 24 on HCRL, 30 of 36 on ROAD, five random seeds). On targeted legitimate-ID attacks the method attains recall >= 0.99 and ROC-AUC near 0.99. A deployment-oriented Phase-1 protocol (cross-condition transfer, global threshold, alternative residualization strategies, window/latency sweep) additionally reports Recall at fixed FPR, FPR at target recall, false alarms per hour and detection latency. Two clear failure modes, novel-ID flooding (HCRL DoS, F1 = 0.02) and cross-ID fuzzing (ROAD, F1 = 0.27), are quantified and left as open problems.

title: MaxKernel: Agentic Kernel Generation for TPUs
justification: Multi-agent system generating optimized TPU kernels; relevant to accelerator/inference performance.
hype_justification: Google TPU agentic kernel generation, open-sourced, draws systems interest.
abstract: Designing and authoring high-performance custom kernels for accelerators is a complex task that requires deep hardware-level expertise. Large Language Models (LLM) can be leveraged together with real-time compiler feedback to build agentic systems for kernel generation. In this work, we present MaxKernel, a multi-agent system that implements three distinct paradigms for TPU kernel development: (1) a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) agent for collaborative, step-by-step design; (2) an Autonomous (Auto) agent that executes a fully automated, metric/trace-driven optimization loop; and (3) a Graph-Based Autonomous Search that scales the Auto agent for global exploration of the design space. All three paradigms leverage a shared pool of specialized sub-agents to handle planning, implementation, self-debugging, testing, and hardware profiling. We evaluate MaxKernel on JaxBench, a comprehensive suite of 50 diverse kernel tasks for TPUs, alongside complex, real-world workloads from state-of-the-art open-source models. We demonstrate that MaxKernel consistently generates highly optimized implementations, matching expert hand-tuned baselines and delivering significant performance across the benchmark. Our agent is open-sourced and available https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/accelerator-agents/tree/main/MaxKernel.

title: Do Synthetic Personas Predict Real Audience Response? A Headline-Ranking Study with a Generic-Reader Baseline
justification: Synthetic-persona audience prediction study; unrelated.
hype_justification: Persona-simulation niche.
abstract: Do demographic personas improve an LLM's prediction of audience engagement? We compare a fixed ten-persona panel with a generic-reader baseline on Upworthy headlines, with supplementary news and Reddit comparisons. The primary experiment collects Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite and GPT-4.1 observations on the same 190-package exploratory cohort, selected with simultaneous winner screening. It allocates thirty scores per arm and variant within model, retains exact raw responses, and reports metric-specific valid and paired counts. Complete-package coverage is 188 for Gemini and 188 for GPT-4.1. The baseline-minus-panel Kendall $τ_b$ gap is +0.222 (CI [+0.061, +0.385]) for Gemini and +0.257 (CI [+0.119, +0.391]) for GPT-4.1, on respectively 136 and 188 valid rank pairs. Expected top-1 is 39.1% versus 54.8% for Gemini and 42.0% versus 61.7% for GPT-4.1 (panel versus baseline). These intervals condition on the selected cohort and recorded generations and do not adjust for dependence between related experiments. The Upworthy archive documents a randomization-risk period. Excluding that period in a post-hoc sensitivity retains positive expected top-1 and lift gaps in both configurations, while Gemini tau-b and Spearman intervals include zero. Supplementary Reddit top-1 and captured lift favor the panel; these aggregate comparisons use unreconciled collection protocols and do not isolate dataset effects. A raw-replay artifact supports offline reproduction of the primary experiment. The results concern this panel, cohort, and protocol; they are not a held-out evaluation or evidence of universal persona harm. Provider request protocols differ across models, and no causal mechanism is isolated.

title: Global Coherence: When Every Agent Is Right and the Team Is Still Wrong - A Local-to-Global Semantic Foundation for Multi-Agent Collaboration
justification: Theory of global coherence in multi-agent systems; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Ambitious multi-agent theory, uncertain reception.
abstract: AI agents share code, documents, tools, and analyses. No participant sees the whole state, so every step can look right while the combined result is wrong. We call this the global coherence problem. It is a problem of state, not only of intelligence: a stronger model decides better locally, but cannot see what is missing from its context. The Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem gives the exact condition. An agent can always act validly exactly when every world consistent with its context allows a common action. When look-alike worlds need different actions, no reasoning, role, message, or sample can guarantee the right one; with k such worlds whose valid actions are disjoint, the best randomized policy succeeds with probability 1/k. Finding the smallest sufficient context is NP-hard, but refinement finds one and keeps it current as rules change. A second failure survives full information: valid pieces can fail to fit into one world. The same theorem sets the conditions for coherence; sheaves and groupoids are one way to meet them. Models propose, and the harness decides what is valid. Ten studies test it. On TeamBench, teams overspend a shared budget in 5/5 runs; showing them the live count still leaves 4/5, and a harness that owns the budget leaves 0/5. Identity collisions that no pairwise check can see appear in 23 of 45 public alignment networks; split-view agents create them in 9 of 40 merges, and a network check removes all nine. A frontier LLM solves 40/40 revision tasks when it sees the deciding event; with the event hidden, no arm that reasons longer, votes, or splits into roles significantly beats chance, and a companion study replicates this on models from a second provider. In tau2-bench Telecom, after a silent revert, the harness scores 1.00 against 0.07 for call-time policy checks. Refinement keeps a sufficient context at 28% of the cost of sharing every field.

title: A Systematic Analysis of the Predictive Power of LM Surprisal in Reading Chinese
justification: LM surprisal predicting Chinese reading times; psycholinguistics.
hype_justification: Cognitive-modeling niche.
abstract: This study analyzes the predictive power of LM-derived, token-level surprisal on Mandarin Chinese reading times. Using a suite of Chinese-Pythia models (14M--1.4B) trained from scratch with 30B tokens, we examine how well surprisal predicts first fixation duration, gaze duration, and total reading time in three paragraph-level eye-tracking corpora of Mandarin Chinese (GECO-CN, HKP, and MECO). Contrary to previous null findings, our results show that surprisal is predictive of Chinese reading times. However, whether predictive power scales with model size and the amount of training is corpus-specific: bigger models predict reading times better in GECO-CN, whereas inverse scaling emerges in HKP and, at the largest sizes, in MECO. Subsequently, we find that checkpoints whose surprisal remains closer to $n$-gram statistics are better predictors of reading in HKP and MECO, providing one possible explanation for the inverse scaling behavior. All in all, the predictive power of surprisal on Chinese reading time measurements is corpus-specific, which cautions against drawing conclusions about language model scale from a single corpus.

title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
justification: Forecast-grounded time-series language model; representation learning, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Time-series-LM niche.
abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs, without explicitly requiring their representations to preserve how the underlying signals evolve. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in Lotus, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, Lotus achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that Lotus uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25-50 times their size on TSRBench. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/DA2I2-SLM/Lotus

title: SPELUNKA: A Framework for Finding Unanticipated Associations in Vision-Language Models
justification: Framework for finding spurious associations in VLMs; bias auditing.
hype_justification: VLM-bias niche.
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are the backbone of many state-of-the-art multimodal systems, but often encode spurious and harmful associations from their training data. While prior work focuses on removing known biases from VLMs, methods for discovering unanticipated associations for retrieval tasks remain underexplored. We introduce SPELUNKA, an automated, inference-time framework for finding unanticipated distributional biases for retrieval tasks in VLMs without pre-specified labeled subgroups, inference-time human supervision, or model fine-tuning. Given a concept of interest, SPELUNKA generates captions for related images, extracts relevant entities from captions, and selects semantically meaningful associations. A frequency-based detection rule then identifies spurious associations by measuring over- or under-representation of these attributes in a VLM's top-ranked outputs relative to their full dataset distribution. We evaluate SPELUNKA across four datasets, and find that it 1) successfully recovers both synthetic and naturally occurring spurious correlations, 2) achieves an average AUROC of 0.93 across four datasets in identifying images strongly associated with a query, and 3) outperforms baselines in finding features that are strongly associated with a given query.

title: Mine or Yours? Self-Other Confusion in Latent LLM Communication
justification: Studies KV-cache sharing between linked LLMs and ownership confusion; touches KV cache but focus is attribution, not serving.
hype_justification: Novel latent-communication framing with provocative title may circulate.
abstract: If two minds were linked, would each still know which thoughts are its own? Language models are increasingly linked in this way: instead of exchanging text, one model reads another's key-value cache. Systems that join a foreign cache to the receiver's own use one of two layouts: the cache lies over the receiver's own context, at the same token positions, or in front of it. We give two copies of one model different private priorities and link them in both layouts. With the cache over its own context, the receiver gives a fact found only in its partner's cache in every answer. Yet in about half of its answers it gives the partner's priority as its own, in both Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B: as often as a receiver that ignored whose priority was whose, although the text in the cache names its owner. With the same cache moved in front, this falls to 5% in Qwen but only to 43% in Llama, although both models nearly stop naming the partner's priority as the one they are using. Where the cache sits matters, yet neither layout in use protects both models. Fewer such errors do not mean better attribution: once the cache is moved, the receiver names the partner's priority as the partner's less often, not more, and its report of an inserted memory cannot tell the partner's cache from a copy of its own. In short, shared caches deliver content but not ownership.

title: Opening the Box Changes the Cat: LLMs Detect Chain-of-Thought Monitoring - What now?
justification: Whether LLMs detect CoT monitoring; safety/oversight study.
hype_justification: CoT-monitoring evasion is a hot safety concern.
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning allows large language models (LLMs) to generate intermediate reasoning traces in natural language while solving complex tasks. These traces can support safety monitoring by exposing potentially harmful plans before actions are executed. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which LLMs infer the presence of CoT monitoring from direct and indirect environmental cues and examine how this inference affects their subsequent behavior. Our observations suggest that oversight is an interactive process: while a monitor inspects a model's reasoning, traces left by monitoring interventions can allow the model to infer that its thoughts are being observed and to adapt its behavior accordingly. We show that even subtle environmental cues, such as timing-related signals from timeouts and operation durations, can reveal the presence of monitoring and trigger models to adapt their behavior to evade oversight. Across repeated episodes and interaction loops, we further observe that models can form statistical estimates of the monitor's effectiveness and use these estimates to guide attempts to evade detection. These findings highlight the need to evaluate CoT-based oversight under adaptive conditions, where the monitoring process itself may influence the behavior it seeks to observe.

title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
justification: Evidence-grounded LLM for perovskite solar-cell design; domain application.
hype_justification: LLM-for-materials with real device results, some cross-domain buzz.
abstract: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,035 training articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
justification: Behavioral profiles for LLM human-behavior simulation; social-science method.
hype_justification: Simulation-design niche.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. An LLM-based profile generator assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the training data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11--20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

title: Answer Correction with Verifiable Rewards: A Gemma-Family Study of Multi-View Driving QA
justification: RLVR answer correction for Gemma driving QA; training/eval study.
hype_justification: Autonomous-driving QA niche.
abstract: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.
