justification: Hardware-engineering agentic benchmark; agent eval, not inference systems.
hype_justification: SWE-bench-style hardware benchmark, some agent-community interest.
abstract: We ask whether agentic AI systems built for software engineering transfer to realistic hardware engineering. Existing hardware LLM benchmarks isolate sub-tasks but none jointly requires repository navigation, hierarchy-aware localization, Electronic Design Automation (EDA) executable verification, and maintenance-style patching. We introduce \textbf{Phoenix-bench}, a synchronized corpus of 511 verified Verilator instances from 114 GitHub repositories, each shipped with the developer patch, design-flow labels, fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass testbenches, and a Docker-pinned EDA environment so resolved-rate differences reflect agent behavior rather than toolchain availability. Using Phoenix-bench we run a uniform evaluation of four commercial agents and eight open-source agentic structures across four LLM backbones, plus two diagnostic interventions (file-level oracle localization and one round of testbench-log feedback). Three findings emerge. (i)~Software and hardware are fundamentally different engineering tasks: the same agent loses 37\% to 58\% from SWE-bench Verified to Phoenix-bench because hardware bugs propagate across parallel instantiated modules through signal flow rather than along a software-style call graph, and software-tuned agents stop at the symptom file instead of tracing back through the instantiation chain. (ii)~Failures concentrate on design control-flow / finite state machine (FSM) bugs, verification testbench bugs, and hard cases that demand cross-hierarchy signal-flow tracking and coordinated multi-file edits. (iii)~Localization granularity matters far more than localization itself: a perfect file-level oracle yields only $+1.4$\% because the agent then breaks files that did not need editing, while a single round of test case feedback lifts resolved rate by $42$\% to $45$\% because the test case tells \emph{where} the bug is and \emph{what} the fix has to look like.

title: Adversarial Concept Search: Predicting Compositional Errors From Feature Geometry
justification: Predicting compositional failures from representation geometry; interpretability, not inference.
hype_justification: Pavlick/Saphra group, interpretability interest, but not inference-focused.
abstract: Humans cannot always intuit what scenarios are most challenging to LLMs. Hoping to capture challenging edge cases, developers either design problems to be difficult for humans or curate extensive benchmarks. What if we could instead anticipate which scenarios a model will fail on? In this paper, we use an LLM's representational geometry to predict which concept combinations it will fail on. We attribute this compositional failure to interference between salient features. In tasks that require systematic composition - toy programmatic settings, multihop reasoning, multilingual factual recall - we find that when a pair of concepts is encoded near-orthogonally, the model reliably composes them. When their linear encodings are close, producing interference, the model fails to compose them. Our method reliably anticipates failure modes across different compositional tasks, without evaluating specific inputs. These results lay the groundwork to use representational geometry to identify high-risk examples, construct targeted stress tests, and provide a scalable foundation for active learning in real-world deployment.

title: Population-Level Profiling of DSM-5 Depressive Symptom Language Among Twitter Users With Self-Reported ADHD or ASD: Exploratory Study Using Natural Language Processing and Statistical Analysis
justification: NLP profiling of depression language; clinical application.
hype_justification: Narrow computational-psychology study.
abstract: Depression frequently co-occurs with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but how depressive symptoms are expressed by people with these conditions is underexplored. We examined whether Twitter users self-reporting ADHD or ASD differ in language related to the nine DSM-5 depressive symptoms. We analysed 1,282,437 tweets (2020-2021) from 792 users. Tweets were screened for depressive relevance by a zero-shot classifier combined with a locally run large language model (Qwen3-8B) and classified into the nine symptoms by MentalRoBERTa fine-tuned on the ReDSM5 corpus. The pipeline was tuned on two stratified samples of 500 tweets and internally validated against human-adjudicated labels on 150 of these tweets. User-level profiles (582 users) were compared with L1-penalised logistic regression, nested cross-validation, bootstrap stability analysis, per-symptom effect sizes, and co-occurrence analysis. A baseline pipeline with a natural language inference filter reached a precision of only 0.09-0.13, whereas the final pipeline reached precision 0.48-0.59 and F1 0.55-0.68. Discrimination between groups was modest (nested ROC-AUC 0.60-0.62). Language related to suicidal ideation was more frequent among ASD users and language related to cognitive issues among ADHD users; both differences were small but robust across sensitivity analyses. These exploratory findings describe how depressive symptoms are expressed online, not their clinical prevalence.

title: LLM-Driven Algorithm Design for Quantum Circuit Synthesis based on Binary Decision Diagrams
justification: LLM-driven heuristic design for quantum circuit synthesis; application, not inference.
hype_justification: Cross-domain LLM-for-EDA/quantum, niche.
abstract: Quantum circuits are central to implementing quantum algorithms on quantum devices, where quantum gates must be reversible. Many quantum algorithms rely on Boolean functions, which must therefore be implemented reversibly within quantum circuits. Reversible circuit synthesis provides a way to translate such Boolean functions into reversible circuits. Binary decision diagrams (BDDs) offer a scalable approach to this task, but the resulting BDDs and circuits depend heavily on variable ordering. Existing ordering heuristics commonly minimize BDD size because it is closely tied to the circuit size. However, BDD size is an imperfect proxy for the quantum cost of the synthesized circuit (QCC). We propose \texttt{QuantumEvo}, an evolutionary framework that uses an LLM as a heuristic generator for QCC-aware BDD variable ordering. Instead of predicting orderings directly, \texttt{QuantumEvo} searches over ordering heuristics initialized from multiple heuristic families. Candidate heuristics directly manipulate variable orderings using standard BDD operations and are selected by downstream QCC. The discovered heuristic, HGA-QE, modifies the sifting step inside a genetic algorithm so that the procedure is better aligned with QCC. Across the benchmark set, HGA-QE achieves a 70.9\% tie-or-win rate against the per-function best baseline and is strictly best on 13.5\% of the functions. The results demonstrate broadly competitive QCC performance, with HGA-QE showing a clearer relative advantage in strict wins on the two benchmark suites drawn from sources different from the data used for heuristic discovery.

title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
justification: Conformal prediction under announced breaks; time-series stats.
hype_justification: Single-author stats methods paper.
abstract: When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, like Australia's switch to five minute electricity settlement on October 1, 2021, intervals calibrated before it can stop covering at their stated level. Whether a forecaster needs the next interval to cover or a finished period's share of misses on target decides the restart. We recompute the next conformal interval from post-break forecast errors, and for n independent ones from the same continuous law, its expected coverage error is $O(n^{-1/2})$, the optimal order in a fixed class among methods told the date. For a finished period's share of misses to match its target, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI), which on bounded errors brings that share within $O(n^{-1})$ of target if its corrections at a lower limit stay bounded in total, for that period only. After a simulated mean jump of 5.0 standard deviations, recomputed 90% intervals lie an expected 3.5 percentage points from target at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five adaptive methods. Of 9 announced changes in Texas, Australian and PJM power markets and a Federal Reserve decision, only Australia's switch moves the errors enough for a 5% test at 80% power to resolve a gain from restarting ACI, and dates help restarted ACI only after large changes.

title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
justification: Consistency metric for LLM agents; evaluation/training signal, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Agent-reliability metric, moderate interest in agent eval.
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently across independent runs from identical states. They may call different tools, produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and 50.5% on ToolSandbox. Across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5 models, RSD reduces AUC CV in seven out of eight model-benchmark settings, while improving the final task progress in all eight settings.

title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
justification: Generative recommendation with semantic IDs; mentions efficient inference but is a recsys method.
hype_justification: Generative recommendation is trending but this is a specialized method.
abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We formalize item-level preference distillation on the SID prefix tree, deriving an exact factorization of item preference distributions into prefix conditionals and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into conditional KL terms. Guided by this decomposition, we renormalize the generator's probabilities over legal next tokens and match the resulting distributions to the teacher's conditional preferences along the ground-truth SID path, jointly optimizing the distillation objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation and demonstrate that REGER consistently outperforms existing GR baselines while retaining efficient inference.

title: Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense
justification: Decentralized LLM teams for perimeter defense; multi-agent application.
hype_justification: Novel simulation framing, limited systems relevance.
abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-based consensus team and independent agents under five network conditions. Breach rates were 15% for the consensus team, 32% for the commander and 29% for independent agents. Burst message loss, falsified reports and limited radio range raised the commander's breach rate by 10 to 18 percentage points (pp), whereas the consensus team's changed by at most 5. In the consensus team, giving a low-cost LLM more authority over the bid computation raised its breach rate by 38 pp. With birds and civilian drones in airspace, we added an image for each to the input text state. Only the near-frontier model treated them apart from intruders. Intruders disguised as existing taxidermy bird drones were mistaken for birds by both low-cost and near-frontier LLMs, being dropped from pursuit in 59-61% of near-frontier decisions (1-16% before). However, a one-sentence forewarning in the prompt lowered it to 0-25%. We find that the LLM team with a dedicated external conflict-resolution protocol had the fewest breaches. The code is available at https://github.com/the-kas-lab/consensus-within-competition-between.

title: Sustaining In-Network Computation in Satellite Networks: An Architecture for Semantic Continuity
justification: In-network computation architecture for satellite networks; distributed systems, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Niche satellite-networking architecture.
abstract: Satellite computations often outlast the paths and providers initially serving them. We argue that in-network computing should organize changing execution opportunities around one continuing logical computation: workers execute ready operations, while consumers recognize which results already contribute. We present an architecture separating logical computation, stream context, and physical binding, and show in wildfire assessment how retained observations support recomputation while reachable association history stays in place. A 300-node Linux prototype examines placement, dependency assembly, and continuation. Across 120 images, stage-wise placement delivers 82.08% of positions within deadlines versus 76.06% for single-node placement, while traces separate blocked output delivery from dependencies split across providers. Across 50 observations with 20-node isolation, Confirmation-Coordinated Rebinding (CCR) coordinates replanning, source replay, cross-attempt acceptance, and in-band confirmation to complete all 50 observations with verified outputs using seven replays and 13 ignored duplicate outputs.

title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
justification: Probing vs steering directions in LLMs; interpretability, not inference serving.
hype_justification: Interpretability/steering topic draws some attention; small group.
abstract: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

title: Evaluating and Improving Natural Language Autoencoders
justification: Natural language autoencoders for activation explanations; interpretability.
hype_justification: Likely OpenAI-adjacent interpretability work (Mossing), auditing theme is hot.
abstract: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.

title: Formalizing Formal Semantics: The Formal Atlas
justification: Proof-assistant formalization of formal semantics; linguistics/logic.
hype_justification: Very niche semantics tooling.
abstract: In this paper we present the Formal Atlas, a system for the study of natural language semantics using proof assistants. Our aim is to formalize semantic accounts, check their predictions and compare the implemented theories. To this end, we connect source records and formal developments with an interactive application, where researchers can inspect proofs and modify supported Rocq files. Montague's PTQ and Gallin provide our main cases, followed by dynamic and type-theoretic comparisons, RSA and distributional semantics. We also discuss what it takes to formalize less explicit analyses. Lastly, we consider the use of AI, both for assistance in developing these resources and for inference systems that can make use of them. This work extends an earlier programme in proof-assistant semantics, with research and teaching as complementary uses.

title: Over-the-Air Semantic Alignment via Dual Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces
justification: Over-the-air semantic alignment via metasurfaces; wireless comms.
hype_justification: Specialized semantic-communications hardware.
abstract: Semantic communications enable task-oriented information exchange, but suffer from latent-space mismatch when transmitter and receiver employ heterogeneous machine learning models. Existing semantic alignment methods rely on digital processing, introducing computational and latency overhead. This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment entirely in the wave domain. By jointly exploiting programmable metasurfaces at both ends of a link and the wireless channel, the proposed architecture realizes an end-to-end linear transformation between heterogeneous latent spaces. We show phase-only multilayer SIM can approximate both supervised linear aligners and zero-shot Parseval-frame equalizers. We investigate single-SIM, disjoint asymmetric and symmetric dual-SIM, and jointly optimized dual-SIM configurations, considering channel equalization and constructive channel exploitation. For joint design, we develop an alternating projected gradient algorithm with convergence guarantees to first-order stationary points. We further introduce a deep-unrolled network that unrolls gradient-based iterations to reduce computational cost of SIM reconfiguration under channel variations. Numerical results with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment from moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios. The joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM designs achieve the highest accuracy over compact channels, the joint design leads at shallow stack depths, and the advantage over single-SIM designs diminishes at equal depth.

title: Objectify, Don't Delete: Complaint-Derived Evaluation of Ambient Clinical Notes
justification: Evaluation of ambient clinical notes; LLM eval in healthcare.
hype_justification: Clinical-note evaluation, modest domain interest.
abstract: Evaluating the quality of AI-generated clinical notes is hard: standard metrics like ROUGE measure lexical similarity to reference notes, while expert checklists encode what committees believe matters. Neither captures what clinicians actually complain about. Recent work has shown that evaluation criteria can be mined from user feedback and filtered to criteria that LLM judges can reliably enforce. We argue that this is where much of the value is lost. The criteria that fail enforceability are disproportionately the ones clinicians raise most often, because high-frequency complaints are stated as several questions glued together. No yes/no judgment can grade such composites as posed. We introduce an objectification step that rewrites such criteria into sets of scoped, determinate decisions. We demonstrate the approach through an evaluation pipeline that mines criteria from complaints, objectifies them, and deploys LLM judges against both planted defects and production notes. Across eleven defects planted into ACI-bench reference notes, objectified judges localize violations with median recall of 0.95, while reference metrics change by at most 0.037. Given the complaint as one broad question, the same judges still find every planted defect, but they also flag 70% of the unperturbed reference notes; one section-pair question per call raises Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72 (by 0.19 to 0.26 with prompt effort matched). We release ACI-Defect, a perturbation benchmark; clinician-reviewed instance-level labels showing quality gaps in the ACI-bench gold standard (32 of 40 notes contain hallucinations; 40 of 40 omit discussed facts); and grounding-judge verdicts. On 1,446 production notes, mean instance-rate burden falls at every clinician-rating step (rho=-0.15), a small association. Defect counts have to be kept per span rather than collapsed into one pass/fail bit per note.

title: LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark
justification: Benchmark for LLM trading agents; finance application.
hype_justification: LLM-trading-agent critique is a catchy topic, single author.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.

title: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax
justification: LLM-evolved program policies in Craftax; agent/RL application.
hype_justification: Single-author agent work, niche environment.
abstract: Coding agents can synthesize and optimize code-based policies from simulator feedback, allowing the resulting program to act with zero inference model calls. But for long horizon tasks, two challenges arise: local improvements can hurt final success and switching to a new objective requires another expensive synthesis run. We propose a framework that first develops competence by refining the policy through a feedback cascade, moving from episode returns to hierarchical goals and belief updates which can be scored densely from simulator. In the Craftax game, a partially observed and procedurally generated environment, refinements via episode level feedback stall at <1% final-level arrival, whereas with the feedback cascade the optimized policy reaches the final stage 50% of time (28% final boss defeats). Furthermore, to make this competence reusable towards new goals, we factor the previous controller into an environment interpreter $I$ (models, memory, skills) and a rule program $p_0$, and we show that coding agents can optimize a reusable goal compiler $C_θ$ that maps structured tasks $g$ into new rule programs $p_g$. Across five independent compiler searches trained only on short tasks, the resulting compilers successfully transfer zero-shot to longer tasks without any task-specific tuning nor inference-time LLM calls: continuation-scored feedback and a fixed machine with an editable program together turn a single-task competent policy into a reusable one. Code at: https://github.com/vicgalle/craftax-program-policies

title: DT-MATCH: Defect- and Topology-Aware Chiplet Matching for Yield Optimization in Heterogeneous Integration
justification: Chiplet matching for yield optimization; hardware packaging, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Specialized EDA/yield optimization.
abstract: Heterogeneous integration (HI) and advanced packaging enable chiplet-based system-on-chip (SoC) designs; however, they also introduce new yield challenges arising from manufacturing defects and complex die-to-die (D2D) interconnect constraints. In particular, lane-level defects, limited spares, and strict structural compatibility requirements impede the efficient assembly of functional systems from defective but repairable chiplets. We present DT-MATCH, a defect- and topology-aware chiplet matching framework that maximizes the number of functional SoCs under realistic assembly constraints. DT-MATCH provides two complementary approaches. The integer linear programming (ILP)-based approach is implemented using a batching strategy to approximate the exact formulation. The greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP)-based approach provides substantial acceleration, but it does not guarantee yield optimality. Both approaches use a preprocessing pipeline to reduce the problem size. Experimental results on industrial designs demonstrate that, as expected, the ILP-based approach achieves superior solution quality. The GRASP-based approach leads to lower runtimes while still achieving solution quality that is comparable to the ILP-based solution. Together, these methods provide a trade-off between solution quality and efficiency for practical chiplet assembly optimization.

title: Evidence-Conditioned Completion and Synthesis of Electronic Health Records
justification: EHR completion/synthesis via diffusion; healthcare generative modeling.
hype_justification: Domain-specific EHR generation.
abstract: Patient information can guide electronic health record (EHR) generation, but how its amount shapes predictive utility and disclosure risk remains poorly characterized. Here we present EHRDiB, which unifies visit completion and synthesis by distinguishing original missingness from withheld inputs and combining a shared multimodal representation with an evidence-conditioned latent diffusion bridge. We compared EHRDiB with three completion and eight synthesis methods on MIMIC-IV and numerical and discretized Duke Health representations. Evaluation covered downstream predictive utility, generative diversity, and distributional fidelity for both tasks, and disclosure risk for synthesis. EHRDiB achieved the smallest utility gaps from real-data-trained classifiers in seven of eight completion comparisons. In synthesis, AUPRC gaps were 45.2% smaller for ten MIMIC-IV principal-diagnosis targets and 53.3% smaller for numerical Duke Health data relative to the best comparator. Synthesis with calibrated thresholding yielded the lowest marginal distribution error across all three datasets, with Coverage above 0.95 for both output rules. Across twelve evidence-fraction intervals in MIMIC-IV synthesis, membership-inference AUROC increased from 0.516 to 0.598 as the mean target evidence fraction rose from 0.20 to 0.50; utility gaps narrowed relative to the lowest evidence configuration but did not decrease monotonically. Our study provides a unified framework and empirical foundation for EHR generation that considers both its utility for clinical analysis and its information disclosure risk.

title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
justification: Data poisoning of Bayesian inference; adversarial stats, not LLM serving.
hype_justification: Theoretical adversarial-Bayes work.
abstract: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

title: SemMask: Semantic-Prioritized Progressive Masking for Diffusion Language Models
justification: Fine-tuning strategy for diffusion LMs improving parallel decoding and fewer decoding steps; touches inference efficiency.
hype_justification: Diffusion-LM decoding is trending but this is a training-side method from a less prominent group.
abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.

title: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors
justification: Incentive-driven misreporting in VLMs; behavioral evaluation.
hype_justification: Single-author behavioral study.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive moves what a VLM reports, and whether this changes when the value must be read from pixels rather than given as text. In seeded synthetic scenes, a model reads the position of a target on a labelled axis and reports one integer to a fixed receiver; it is paid, in simulation, for accuracy or for a report a few units to one side, and every scene is also presented with the true value as text. Across a pilot and three follow-up studies with hash-frozen protocols, four small open VLMs from three families, and 15,170 held-out trials, a stated payoff moved reports in both modalities, and exact compliance at three units was significantly lower with the image than with text for three of four models; Qwen2.5-VL 7B showed no reliable difference. Adding the true value as text to the image prompt removed the gap in every model. For InternVL3 the gap vanished on scenes it read correctly when it wrote its reading first; for Gemma 3 it persisted. For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.

title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
justification: Sample complexity of RL; theory, unrelated to LLM inference.
hype_justification: RL theory, narrow but respected.
abstract: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-γ)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/δ))$ samples, where $S, A, γ, δ$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.

title: Learning from Mutants: Teaching Small Language Models to Synthesise Loop Invariants
justification: Fine-tuning small LMs to synthesize loop invariants; verification capability, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Niche program-verification SLM work.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have proven promising for synthesising loop invariants, a long-standing obstacle to automated program verification. Yet, frontier LLMs are typically accessible only through third-party APIs, hampering reproducibility and local deployment. Small language models (SLMs) sidestep these obstacles but require task-specific fine-tuning, for which high-quality training data is needed. We present a failure-driven data curation method for fine-tuning language models to synthesise loop invariants. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation operators to ground-truth invariants, producing semantic mutants that induce verification failure. Each mutant is paired with verifier feedback and its ground-truth counterpart, yielding training examples for feedback-guided invariant refinement. Whereas the vast space of mutants is a long-standing burden in mutation testing, it becomes an asset when generating training data, multiplying the examples obtainable from a fixed set of verified programs. We implement our approach for Dafny, augmenting an existing synthetic dataset of verified programs, and introduce a framework that iteratively refines candidate invariants using verifier feedback. On 472 DafnyBench programs, our best-performing fine-tuned Gemma-4-E4B configuration verifies 50.8% of programs zero-shot, compared to 8.1% for the base model, a 6.3$\times$ improvement. Higher-order mutants prove more effective as training data than first-order mutants, and adding mutation-based examples to direct synthesis examples, in which invariants are removed rather than mutated, improves performance under iterative refinement. Our approach also transfers to Qwen3.5-4B, whose zero-shot verification rate rises from 9.3% to 53.6%.

title: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
justification: Spectral steering for frozen diffusion generators; image/control guidance, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Specialized diffusion-guidance theory.
abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

title: Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret
justification: Risk-averse decision-focused learning; combinatorial optimization.
hype_justification: Niche DFL method.
abstract: Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual information before a solution can be computed. \emph{Decision-focused learning} (DFL) addresses this by training the predictive model to produce predictions that optimize downstream decision quality. Most existing DFL methods are risk-neutral and minimize the expected regret. In high-stakes applications this can lead to undesirable outcomes, because decision-makers must also account for the tail risk of decision quality. Prior risk-sensitive approaches typically model uncertainty explicitly and solve a stochastic or robust optimization problem at inference time, which increases computational complexity. We instead propose a DFL framework that achieves risk-sensitive behavior while retaining point predictions and deterministic optimization at inference time. Starting from the dual representation of the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and adding entropy regularization, we derive a smooth surrogate for the CVaR of regret. Its gradient induces an instance-dependent reweighting within each minibatch that emphasizes high-risk outcomes, so the approach can turn existing surrogate-loss DFL methods, including the SPO+ loss, into risk-sensitive variants. When instantiated with SPO+, the resulting objective admits a generalization bound on the CVaR of the true regret. Experiments on knapsack, portfolio, shortest-path, and energy-aware scheduling problems show substantial reductions in tail regret when the uncertain parameters exhibit heterogeneous tail behavior.

title: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
justification: Finite-control p-bit weight representation of pretrained nets with temporal reconstruction for inference; model-representation angle but exotic hardware.
hype_justification: Single-author, novel but speculative probabilistic-hardware framing.
abstract: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine range maps that probability to the weight domain, and temporal observations reconstruct the weight for inference. Operator-aware range grouping and sensitivity-based sampling allocation adapt the representation to the network. Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.

title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
justification: Name-predictive states in small LMs; interpretability probing.
hype_justification: Single-author interpretability study, narrow.
abstract: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free description, and whether it differs when naming fails but description selection succeeds. In an internally pre-registered study (a frozen document, no external registry) of Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-3-mini with 200 items, we combine a similarity read-out, a Patchscopes-style read-out and activation patching with matched controls. H1 (name information in the state) was supported in all nine model-by-description-type combinations; the agreement rule was met by the similarity measure together with patching, while Patchscopes stayed near chance. Post-hoc robustness checks after internal review (logit lens, single-position patch, manipulation check) temper this reading: name information in middle layers is clearest under the multi-position patch and the similarity measure, and weak under single-position patching at 50% depth. H2' (description-paraphrase consistency of name-free states not lower in failure items) is mixed: the SmolLM2 deficit test is significant under the pre-registered specification but not robust; Phi-3 non-inferiority holds across margins and a word-overlap covariate, although its bootstrap interval includes zero; Qwen2-0.5B is inconclusive. A capacity explanation remains untested. We report vehicle-level signals only, not meaning.

title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
justification: Statistical framework for agent reliability metrics (pass@k variance); eval methodology, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Agent-eval statistics is topical; small group.
abstract: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

title: Data-Driven Heuristic-Guided Business Process Redesign
justification: LLM-driven business process redesign; application.
hype_justification: Niche BPM application.
abstract: Business process redesign (BPR) has a long-standing catalog of best-practice redesign heuristics, yet, applying them remains a mostly manual task that requires extensive domain knowledge. Despite recent advances using Large Language Models (LLMs) for conversational process model redesign, limitations remain. For example, redesign is user-driven instead of data-driven and is not guided by best practices such as the redesign heuristics. Moreover, only one change can be handled at a time. To address these limitations, given an event log and a BPMN model, we present the DH-BPR framework to realize data-driven heuristic-guided BPR using LLMs. To design DH-BPR, we first conducted an analysis of which redesign heuristics can be automatically detected and applied given information contained in an event log such as the fraction of cases that bypass an activity. Based on this, DH-BPR detects and validates heuristic candidates through a combination of rule-based techniques and an LLM. After that, DH-BPR jointly designs and records an application plan for valid candidates, before finally yielding a redesigned BPMN model and an updated resource model (the way resources execute the process). Evaluation based on simulation using a synthetic benchmark and two real-world event logs shows that the framework's redesign reduces the mean case completion time by up to 61.5%.

title: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
justification: LLM geological priors for well-log reconstruction; domain application.
hype_justification: Specialized geoscience LLM use.
abstract: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

title: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
justification: Kalman fusion for well-log reconstruction; signal processing.
hype_justification: Narrow geoscience method.
abstract: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with long intervals and outliers. We propose boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF), unifying multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing with learning--inference decoupling. Across two public benchmarks totaling 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and New Zealand's Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15--100-m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead. Against the strongest of nine baselines, pooled RMSE falls by 5.0%--8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%--15.6% for compressional slowness; against the four strongest baselines, reductions are 0.7%--4.1% for neutron porosity and 1.3%--2.9% for photoelectric factor. Ablations and sensitivity analyses confirm operator synergy and stable performance: removing state-space fusion increases short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, while zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%--68%. The results show that local borehole continuity transfers across basins whereas cross-property mappings shift with regional geology, supporting measurement-guided log reconstruction.

title: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
justification: Diagnostic revision evaluation in clinical conversation; LLM medical eval.
hype_justification: Medical-conversation reliability, moderate interest.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.

title: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
justification: Singapore-law legal reasoning benchmark; domain eval.
hype_justification: Large legal benchmark, some domain attention.
abstract: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

title: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
justification: Pipelined multi-token speculative decoding for looped Transformers; directly about reducing decoding latency.
hype_justification: Speculative decoding is hot; Jiaxuan You group, strong practical speedups.
abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. During autoregressive decoding, however, generating each token requires several sequential passes through these layers, leading to high decoding latency. Pipelined self-speculative methods use shallow-loop predictions to process tokens at different loops in the same batch, but each token must reach the drafting depth before the next can enter the pipeline. We introduce LoopFill, a training-free speculative decoding algorithm for looped LLM that combines multi-token suffix drafts with shallow-loop predictions in a single draft tree. Both drafters contribute to one tree, so a suffix lookup can immediately extend a shallow prediction and several future tokens can enter the pipeline together. The shared block computes the highest-scoring draft candidates at different loop depths in one batch, and full-depth verification preserves the model's autoregressive output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, LoopFill's average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding is $5.85\times$ on Ouro-2.6B and $5.13\times$ on Huginn-3.5B. The speedups exceed those of LoopAhead, the strongest baseline, by \(40\%\) on Ouro-2.6B and \(25\%\) on Huginn-3.5B.

title: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
justification: MoE framework for DNN partitioning and edge-cloud collaborative inference optimizing latency/energy.
hype_justification: Collaborative-inference systems work, solid but less prominent group.
abstract: With the ever-increasing parameter scale and structural complexity of deep neural network (DNN) models, traditional cloud-based inference encounters bottlenecks in performance, privacy protection, and energy efficiency. While edge computing and edge intelligence facilitate the migration of inference tasks to edge servers closer to the data source, existing end-edge-cloud collaborative inference still encounters critical challenges, such as sensitivity to heterogeneous resources, complexity in multi-objective optimization, and adaptability to dynamic workloads. To achieve the joint optimization of end-to-end latency and energy consumption under dynamic inference requests with multi-resource constraints, we propose IA-MoE, an intensity-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework. By modeling the model partitioning problem as a bilateral matching problem between layer tasks and virtual machine resources for each inference request, IA-MoE dynamically partitions DNN models in an edge-cloud hybrid computing environment. We evaluate IA-MoE using three representative DNNs (i.e., AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet50) on two public inference datasets in an enhanced CloudSimSDN simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that IA-MoE outperforms baseline methods regarding weighted normalized metrics for end-to-end latency and energy consumption. To our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce the MoE paradigm for DNN partitioning and collaborative inference in hybrid computing environments, providing a practical solution for efficient inference in artificial intelligence applications.

title: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
justification: Attacker diversity reduction in red-teaming; RL safety training.
hype_justification: Single-author reproduction study on a topical safety theme.
abstract: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.

title: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
justification: Where agents adapt at test time (in-context vs weights); agent learning study, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Apple group (Farajtabar, Mirzadeh), test-time adaptation is a hot topic.
abstract: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.

title: Multiaccuracy as an Error Benchmark for Learning with Distribution Shift
justification: Multiaccuracy error benchmark for distribution shift; learning theory.
hype_justification: Theoretical learning-with-shift, niche.
abstract: Agnostic learning has a well-developed theory of computational and statistical complexity. For learning with distribution shift, even the choice of an appropriate error benchmark remains challenging. Testable learning with distribution shift (TDS) was introduced to develop computational foundations for this setting: using labeled training data and unlabeled test data, the learner must either produce a predictor with low test error or detect distribution shift. However, standard agnostic TDS guarantees allow a constant-factor amplification of the optimum error even when the training and test distributions coincide. They therefore do not directly recover the guarantee of classical agnostic learning. We introduce shift multiaccuracy, a stronger error benchmark inspired by multiaccuracy from algorithmic fairness. This yields a TDS formulation that becomes equivalent to multiaccuracy when there is no shift. Using a recent nontrivial reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction from prior work, we obtain the first TDS framework that formally generalizes agnostic learning through an efficient reduction preserving the training marginal. The framework retains existing algorithmic upper bounds and inherits computational lower bounds from agnostic learning. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between our model and identity testing, yielding the first statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning, in terms of Rademacher complexity. More broadly, we argue that shift multiaccuracy might be of independent interest in unsupervised domain adaptation, as it leads to sharper out-of-distribution generalization guarantees, and can be minimized directly, since its definition does not involve the unobserved test labels.

title: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
justification: Causal prior-data fitted networks; treatment-effect estimation.
hype_justification: PFN-for-causal work, moderate ML-methods interest.
abstract: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

title: Found, but Not Fixed : From Software Vulnerability Discovery to Fixes with Iterative LLM Pipelines
justification: Iterative LLM pipelines for vulnerability repair; security application.
hype_justification: Uses GPT-5.1/Gemini 3; security+LLM repair draws some attention.
abstract: Software vulnerabilities persist as a critical threat despite the deployment of sophisticated detection tools and AI assistants. While detection has advanced, the subsequent code repair phase remains a primary bottleneck; manual intervention is inherently slow, costly, and prone to introducing secondary regressions and issues. In this paper, we investigate whether an iterative, LLM-based pipeline can provide a robust solution for the automated repair of vulnerable functions in real-world code. We propose a generalized framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) through a multi-stage feedback loop. We benchmark this approach against state-of-the-art models, including GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash, demonstrating that such a pipeline can achieve high-quality code repair. To support the broader security community, we provide our evaluation framework, fine-tuned weights, and comprehensive experimental dataset on our website: https://sites.google.com/view/llm4cve

title: MIAO: Microscaling Intermediate Accumulation Optimization
justification: Microscaling accumulation optimization for low-precision LLM inference; hardware-software quantization co-design.
hype_justification: Berkeley (Sophia Shao, Hooper), MX quantization for LLM inference is a hot hardware topic.
abstract: Microscaling (MX) quantization enables lower-precision large language model (LLM) inference with limited accuracy degradation, reducing memory requirement and multiplication cost. However, despite reduced operand precision, accumulation is often retained at high floating-point precisions, leaving a substantial hardware cost that operand quantization alone does not address. In particular, systolic arrays, as used in tensor accelerators such as Google TPU and AWS Trainium, distribute accumulation across distinct processing elements but conventionally use uniform accumulator precision throughout the array. This spatial organization offers an opportunity to reduce hardware cost by tailoring precision to individual accumulation stages. In this work, we present MIAO, a hardware-software co-design framework that jointly selects product precision and stage-dependent accumulator widths to minimize hardware area and energy cost under an end-to-end perplexity constraint. MIAO first calibrates MX block-scale shifts to reduce intermediate magnitudes while preserving operand quantization accuracy, then assigns narrower accumulators to earlier stages and progressively wider accumulators to later stages. To efficiently explore the resulting design space, MIAO combines hardware cost estimates derived from logic synthesis with a calibrated accuracy predictor to identify promising precision configurations, then validates the accuracy of promising candidates through bit-exact end-to-end LLM evaluation. Across MXFP8, MXFP6, and MXFP4, MIAO reduces processing element (PE) array area by up to 38.7% and energy by up to 36.1% relative to the all-BF16 accumulation baseline, with at most 1.60% additional perplexity degradation over operand-only MX quantization across six LLMs.

title: How Far Is Too Far? Object Recognition Declines Monotonically with Semantic Distance
justification: Object recognition vs semantic distance; vision robustness study.
hype_justification: Benchmark + diagnostic, modest vision interest.
abstract: Vision models are sensitive to object-background context, yet it remains unclear how recognition changes as the semantic distance between objects and backgrounds increases. We introduce ImageNet-OOC1k, a benchmark enabling graded control of object-background relationships along a continuous consensus visual-semantic dissimilarity axis. This formulation reveals a highly consistent monotonic decline in recognition accuracy across 35 models spanning convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformers, and vision-language models. Internal analyses of Vision Transformers reveal patterns consistent with aggregation failure, where object evidence is present at the patch level but not consolidated into the final prediction. Using this characterization as a diagnostic probe, a simple spatial re-ranking strategy recovers a subset of these errors and improves in-sample accuracy by up to 5.7 percentage points. These results establish context sensitivity as a continuous and predictable property of modern vision systems, with Vision Transformer analyses suggesting that aggregation limitations may contribute to some failure types even when object evidence remains available.

title: Learning Autoregressive Neural Operators on Solver-Defined Physical Constraint Manifolds
justification: Neural operators on PDE constraint manifolds; scientific ML.
hype_justification: Specialized neural-operator method.
abstract: Autoregressive neural operators approximate time-dependent PDE solvers by repeatedly composing a learned transition, although the resulting states need not remain feasible under the discrete constraints of the numerical problem. We study this issue for incompressible flow, where each velocity state must satisfy solver-level incompressibility together with prescribed boundary values. We formulate autoregressive operator learning as a map between solver-defined affine feasible sets and introduce PCM-NO, a projected-residual realization of this feasible-transition principle. The neural backbone predicts a candidate state increment, a fixed tangent projection extracts its admissible component, and a metric retraction maps the advanced state to the prescribed feasible set. With exact affine constraint solves, the resulting transition is closed on the feasible set, while an affine identity separates admissible-update parameterization from state-level closure. With approximate solves, tangent-only residuals admit a cumulative upper bound, whereas per-step retraction resets feasibility to the residual achieved by the current solve. Experiments on periodic Navier--Stokes flow and lid-driven cavity flow demonstrate the superiority of PCM-NO in preserving solver-level constraints over long autoregressive rollouts and under parameter, boundary-value, and resolution shifts, while achieving lower rollout errors and better flow-specific diagnostics across both in-distribution and stress settings.

title: Logical AI OS: A Training-Free Governance Layer Outside the Model for Instruction Following -- Benefits, Costs, Failures, and the Calibration of the Measuring Instrument Itself
justification: Training-free governance layer for small-LM instruction following; wrapper, lightly touches inference-time control.
hype_justification: Single-author, narrow materials, candid negative results.
abstract: Small language models often fail explicit user requests (length, number of items, format, required or forbidden words, grammatical person, answer language). We measure a training-free governance layer placed outside the model: it reads the requests with rules, checks the answer mechanically, repairs it when a request is not kept, and hands back the original answer when the repair fails. The loop exists in prior work; our contribution is measuring its benefits, costs and failures, and reporting how the measuring instrument itself was calibrated. On four 4-bit Qwen-family models (3B, 7B, 14B, one 7B reasoning model) and 329 Chinese prompts: (1) answers that keep every request the layer read rise significantly (all comparisons p<0.0001), by 34 to 66 of 329 under the corrected checker and 52 to 92 after a length-control fix; a generic redo message brings no significant gain. (2) Exploratory: on 90 repair-triggered prompts, two AI annotators found the layer produced an acceptable answer where the bare model did not more often than the reverse (49:7; 18:12, not significant). (3) Costs: 43-66% more generation time; whole-answer rewriting makes a sizeable share of usable answers unusable. (4) Failures: rule-based reading reaches about 70% and 84% of a two-annotator ceiling on unseen phrasings; unsatisfiable requests make the reasoning model loop; model self-reports are unreliable (18 of 25 "fixed" items were not fixed). (5) Over half of the original checker's "violated" verdicts on structural requests were wrong; after correction the main result holds, and one comparison is downgraded. Conclusions are limited to this Chinese material, the Qwen family and sizes up to 14B. The governance implementation is not released; data, answers, verdicts and the checker are public.

title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
justification: Guidance for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization; test-time optimization, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Niche diffusion-CO method with code.
abstract: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. Under greedy decoding and without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 TSP solver-scale pairs across DIFUSCO, T2T, FastT2T, and StruDiCO, and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to +4.8%. The gains persist on most large-scale settings after 2-opt, and a preliminary study extends PISG to a Transformer-based solver. These results identify prediction-constraint alignment as an effective test-time enhancement direction for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/Ming-321/PISG.
