Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. Their errors pick the real-world outcome, the gap is largest where the game leaves a scene unchanged, and reasoning traces state the game's rule, then answer by reality. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.

title: UNIFY: Unified Learning with One Model via Batch Norm Switching
justification: Single model across datasets via batch-norm switching for CNNs; not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Vision multi-task consolidation niche.
abstract: Neural networks are typically trained separately for individual datasets or tasks, resulting in many task-specific models. This redundancy increases memory footprint, deployment costs, and energy consumption limiting their scalability. We propose UNIFY, a unified learning framework that enables a single model to jointly learn and perform inference across multiple datasets via Batch Normalization Switching (BNS). Instead of maintaining separate models for each dataset, UNIFY shares the parameter-intensive backbone while maintaining dataset-specific BN statistics and parameters, along with dataset-specific classification heads. We validate our framework using five datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) across six Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) of different sizes (SqueezeNet 1.1, WideResNet-40-2, WideResNet-16-8, ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50). Notably, a single UNIFIED ResNet-34 trained on these datasets achieves accuracies of 99.53%, 94.84%, 96.12%, 80.32%, and 67.67%, respectively, outperforming the average performance of the corresponding independently trained task-specific models while reducing the memory footprint by approximately 4.94x, from 428.30 MB (five separate models) to 86.71 MB (one unified model). UNIFY aims not only to consolidate (K) models into a single model but also to enhance model-effectiveness by leveraging complementary knowledge across datasets. It paves the way for scalable, efficient, and unified learning capable of handling diverse image classification tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/saktx/UNIFY.

title: Analytical Modeling and Optimal GPU Provisioning for Disaggregated LLM Inference
justification: Analytical model for optimal prefill/decode GPU provisioning in disaggregated LLM inference, validated on vLLM.
hype_justification: Disaggregated prefill/decode provisioning is a hot serving topic.
abstract: We present OSplit, an exact analytical method that enables efficient partitioning of a GPU L1 domain into prefill and decode workers, including sharding for classical and advanced GPUs. OSplit takes into consideration model parameters, enabling any inference model to be partitioned into prefill and decode workers with a goal of producing the maximum throughput possible. OSplit is based on a capacity model that takes as inputs the model, the loading scheme (batch size, max sequence length), and models an inference serving framework (vLLM) and computes the efficiency of each GPU. For this, we model H100 and GB300 GPUs, and model a scale-up domain, along with FlashAttention-based kernels. OSplit first computes an optimal collective generation policy, which gives inputs to the capacity model that enables optimal split of prefill and decode GPUs. We evaluate our scheme over H100 (NVL8) and GB300 (NVL72) using vLLM inference serving and show throughput, predicted and measured latency, showing near-perfect theoretical-to-measured values over leading LLMs (Llama and Qwen)

title: Multi-Order Passive Macromodeling from Layouts via Nested Port-Hamiltonian Learning
justification: EM/power-network macromodeling via port-Hamiltonian learning; unrelated to LLM inference.
hype_justification: Niche EDA/signal-integrity topic, unknown authors.
abstract: Compact, passive state-space macromodels of interconnects and power-delivery networks are essential for stable transient signal- and power-integrity simulations. However, conventional flows require costly per-layout full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations, while both traditional fitting and prior learning surrogates rely on post-hoc fitting or passivity perturbation that degrades accuracy without guaranteeing convergence. In this work, we propose an end-to-end macromodeling framework that learns directly in the passive space, mapping physical layout graphs to multi-order port-Hamiltonian (pH) macromodels. Specifically, our network encodes each layout graph into unconstrained matrix blocks and assembles them via a complete, prefix-nested pH parameterization that guarantees continuous-frequency passivity and stability by construction, yielding valid $k$-state macromodels via direct state slicing in one forward pass. To train all orders without reference realizations, we supervise the network directly on S-parameters through a progressive order-growth curriculum. Evaluated on 27k unseen test structures from a 270k-structure advanced-packaging dataset, our framework reduces mean S-parameter error by $42\%$ on average (up to $65\%$) over established macromodeling tools fitted to ground-truth EM responses, achieves zero passivity violations across $459{,}000$ exported models, and accelerates macromodel generation by $11{,}000$--$39{,}000\times$ ($36$--$85$~ms per layout).

title: DiscernBench: Evaluating Cooperative Discernment of LLM Agents in Institutional Settings
justification: Benchmark for LLM agent institutional judgment; not about inference systems.
hype_justification: Agent-evaluation benchmark, modest interest, no major lab.
abstract: The deployment of large language models in operational settings demands evaluation of judgment under institutional constraint. We introduce DiscernBench, a benchmark for evaluating cooperative discernment: the ability of an agent to determine whether to comply with, refuse, or escalate a request in an institutional setting. DiscernBench comprises scenarios derived from real-world incident reports across domains such as aviation, law enforcement, and emergency management. We evaluate eight LLMs across three decision-making configurations and analyze both final decisions and the intermediate judgments produced during multi-agent deliberation. Under disagreement, Final Responders exhibit model- and role-dependent aggregation patterns in which a lone specialist recommendation can disproportionately influence the collective decision, a phenomenon we term Minority-Signal Override. Role-specialized multi-agent deliberation raises average over-escalation from 3.79% under direct single-agent judgment to 28.27%, with the direction and magnitude of minority-signal influence varying substantially across models and specialist roles. These results reveal distinct collective decision behaviors that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone. Trustworthy multi-agent systems therefore require evaluating not only individual specialist reasoning, but also how conflicting judgments are transformed into collective decisions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Disha1001/DiscernBench.

title: ArrythML-II: An Optimized TinyML Framework for ECG Arrhythmia Detection and Multi-Class Beat Classification on Wearable Devices
justification: TinyML ECG on wearables; edge inference but not LLM serving/optimization.
hype_justification: Narrow embedded-ML application, niche venue.
abstract: This paper presents ArrythML-II, an optimized TinyML framework for on-device ECG arrhythmia detection and multi-class beat classification on wearable platforms. A systematic hyperparameter optimization framework is developed to identify compact autoencoder architectures for binary ECG arrhythmia detection. A custom scoring mechanism jointly considers detection performance, reconstruction-error thresholds, and model size to guide architecture selection. The framework is further extended to six-class ECG beat classification using a lightweight classifier derived from the optimized autoencoder architecture. Both models are INT8 quantized and deployed using TensorFlow Lite Micro on a custom-developed, battery-operated, single-lead ECG device based on the PSoC~6 microcontroller. The deployed autoencoder and classifier have model sizes of approximately 44~KB and 22~KB, respectively, with end-to-end processing times of 5.1~ms and 4.7~ms per ECG segment. Model inference accounts for 3.95~ms and 1.38~ms of these processing times, respectively. In the refined arrhythmia detection evaluation using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, the autoencoder achieved an accuracy of 84.76\%, precision of 82.68\%, and recall of 77.99\%. The multi-class classifier achieved 82.29\% accuracy, weighted precision of 90.18\%, and weighted recall of 82.29\%. Beyond offline model evaluation, the wearable platform is validated using preloaded ECG segments, live ECG signals, and an ESP32-S3-based ECG emulator that replays annotated MIT-BIH recordings as analog waveforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating optimized TinyML models into wearable platforms for real-time ECG analysis.

title: HighwayVerse: A Chain-of-Inspection Benchmark for Highway Infrastructure Anomaly Understanding
justification: MLLM benchmark for highway inspection; application, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Domain-specific benchmark with dataset release, limited broad appeal.
abstract: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. Meanwhile, current datasets focus primarily on highway pavement defects, falling short of real-world inspection across diverse infrastructure components such as highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, and introduce HighwayVerse. HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world Ground and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) inspection records spanning 100 and 17 anomaly categories, respectively, with 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs. We evaluate 12 open-source and closed-source MLLMs using the chained metric Final, which credits a correct maintenance decision only when all preceding diagnostic stages are completed correctly. Results show that although models achieve relatively high accuracy when initially judging whether an anomaly is present, their markedly lower Final scores expose struggles across downstream recognition, analysis, and decision-making. This discrepancy indicates that current MLLMs do not fully comprehend specific highway anomaly patterns beyond superficial initial judgments. Furthermore, we propose LaneRAG, a training-free retrieval-augmented framework that provides hierarchical reference guidance achieving consistent performance improvements across diverse MLLMs. Our dataset, evaluation benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.

title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
justification: Synthetic EHR memorization audits; privacy not inference systems.
hype_justification: Position paper on auditing, niche healthcare-ML audience.
abstract: Synthetic electronic health record (EHR) generation is increasingly adopting large autoregressive models, yet privacy evaluation has not kept pace, relying heavily on similarity-based heuristics and aggregate metrics that can obscure patient-specific memorisation. We argue that these models should additionally undergo LLM-style memorisation audits at the level of individual patient records. We support this position by comparing membership-inference evaluations across four prominent autoregressive EHR generators, highlighting inconsistent evaluation practices in patient representations and attack procedures. We evaluate trajectory reconstruction from partial context and introduce randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorised associations from clinical generalisation. We examine these methods in a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, creating a controlled setting in which memorisation should be readily detectable. The model systematically recovers training patients' canaries, and their trajectory reconstruction approaches perfect accuracy with increasing context. Held-out patients show no systematic canary recovery, while reconstruction remains low and improves only marginally with additional context. These experiments establish a positive-control baseline for further evaluation of these methods in realistically trained models.

title: When do stored facts become available in looped transformers?
justification: Interpretability of factual recall in looped transformers during inference; not a serving/optimization system.
hype_justification: Qualcomm-affiliated interpretability work, moderate interest.
abstract: Looped transformers do not acquire new knowledge during a forward pass. Prior work shows that they store as many bits in their weights as non-looped models. It remains unclear how recurrence makes this knowledge available during inference. We study this question using synthetic factual recall and multi-hop reasoning, measuring depth-resolved readable information in bits with native readouts and tuned lenses. Under final-loop supervision, single-hop facts become readable progressively: heavier memorization loads delay retrieval despite comparable final readable information. Untied baselines of equal unrolled depth concentrate retrieval near the end of their stacks, whereas looped models expose facts earlier. This delay is not intrinsic to the tested recall tasks: training with supervision and depth-specific readouts at every loop makes near-final information readable after the first loop in all tested configurations. Representational analysis shows value-related structure emerging within states organized by the query key. We then study multi-hop chains whose facts are stored in the weights rather than given in the prompt. Intermediate entities become decodable in chain order, and aligned transitions show next-entity structure developing while current-entity structure remains dominant. Interventions in a released six-recurrence model establish a causal role for these representations. Counterfactual replacements of a probe-defined entity component at a single prompt position redirect downstream bridge entities and the final answer. Conversely, replacements from queries that reach the same entity through different preceding relations, preserving the remaining relation suffix, retain the original answer in over 99.5\% of tested cases. These results distinguish a training-dependent schedule for factual recall from the causal role of retrieved-entity representations in subsequent composition.

title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
justification: Inference-time guidance for diffusion/flow models with reduced backward passes; efficiency-focused but image generation not LLM.
hype_justification: FLUX.2 experiments and efficiency angle give some practical pull.
abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.

title: Beyond Raw IQ: Compact Semantic Representations for Task Oriented Automatic Modulation Classification
justification: Semantic compression for RF modulation classification; unrelated to LLM inference.
hype_justification: Niche wireless-ML topic, low accuracy results.
abstract: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is an important component of modern wireless communication systems, but conventional signal representations can be expensive to store, process, and communicate, particularly under noisy channel conditions. This work investigates whether learned semantic representations can provide a compact alternative to high-dimensional in-phase and quadrature (IQ) representations while retaining robustness to noise. Starting from a 2048-dimensional IQ representation, we evaluate learned semantic representations with dimensions of 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64. Across the evaluated configurations, a 16-dimensional representation provides the strongest overall trade-off between classification performance, robustness, and representation size. The resulting representation achieves a 128x compression ratio and a 99.22% reduction in dimensionality. We further evaluate representation stability across signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), compare semantic representations with a raw-IQ CNN, analyze per-class robustness, and perform five-seed validation. The five-seed evaluation produces an average accuracy of (49.22 +- 0.52)% and Macro-F1 of (49.27 +- 0.53)% across the evaluated SNR range. These results indicate that learned semantic compression can produce a substan- tially smaller representation while preserving useful classification information and improving geometric stability under noise.

title: Pixel Auto-Encoder: Reconstructing Language Model Activations Through Pixel Art
justification: Visualizing LLM activations as pixel art; interpretability, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Novel but exploratory interpretability idea, limited practical draw.
abstract: Interpreting the high-dimensional internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a challenging problem. Recent approaches have explored translating these representations into human-understandable forms, particularly natural language. In this work, we explore the use of images as an alternative target modality for interpreting LLM activations. As a first step toward this goal, we introduce Pixel Auto-Encoder, which converts intermediate LLM activations into $32 \times 32$, 32-color pixel art and reconstructs them for subsequent computation within the model. By encouraging the intermediate representations to resemble predefined concept images, we investigate whether LLM activations can be expressed visually while preserving the model's language capabilities. We find that the model can produce target-aligned images for some concepts, and that replacing pixel representations with concept images can influence next-token predictions. However, we also observe a trade-off between visual alignment and language-model performance, as well as sensitivity to pixel-level changes that are difficult to interpret visually. These findings demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of image-based representations of LLM activations.

title: When Being Wrong Is Right: Reverse-Capability Audio CAPTCHAs through Psychoacoustic Design
justification: Audio CAPTCHA design against audio-LLMs; security, not inference.
hype_justification: Catchy security framing but niche.
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have recently been shown to bypass audio CAPTCHAs designed around limitations of automatic speech recognition. To address this threat, we introduce reverse-capability verification, a general CAPTCHA framework that reverses the conventional human-easy, machine-hard relationship with respect to the physical ground truth. It selects challenges in which stable human perceptual limitations cause the human-reference answer to differ from the physical ground truth, while machine analysis tends toward that truth. Because the verifier accepts the human-reference answer, advanced solver capabilities and resulting improved recovery of the physical ground truth may instead strengthen the human-machine separation. We instantiate the framework through psychoacoustics and design two audio CAPTCHAs: HIPI, a classification task, and YINGCHEN, a counting task, together with their conjunctive composition. Across seven LALMs and eight attack strategies, the maximum observed machine acceptance rates are 19%, 17%, and 3% for HIPI, YINGCHEN, and their composition, respectively, compared with 45-100% for nine prior schemes. A multidimensional human usability study yields corresponding human acceptance rates of 78%, 90%, and 76%, while maintaining competitive efficiency and satisfaction. Further analysis demonstrates that advanced LALMs tend toward physical ground truth. These results show that reverse-capability verification substantially reduces machine acceptance while retaining high human acceptance through an approach different from conventional CAPTCHAs.

title: Does a Frontier Large Language Model Know What It Can Solve? A 100-Conjecture Calibration Study
justification: Calibration of a frontier model on math conjectures; evaluation, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Big-name authors (Arora, Kontorovich) and provocative framing may attract attention.
abstract: How does confidence correlate with actual performance in large language models, when attacking open research-level math problems? We address this question by studying the performance of ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Ultra on a set of 100 open conjectures in geometric analysis. By construction, the model first selected open problems in geometric analysis that it assessed that it had at least a 50\% chance of proving or disproving, and then assigned a probability of success to each question. 13 questions were then excluded after an audit, and the model was asked to resolve the remaining 87 problems. Its mean stated resolution probability was $0.617$, versus an observed rate of $0.103$ (Brier score $0.351$, ECE $0.513$), thereby demonstrating that the model was systematically over-confident in its self-assessment. However, the scores retained ranking signal (AUROC $0.714$). The model was highly overconfident in probability magnitude but did more often than not assign a high probability of success to the problems that it did resolve, than the problems that it did not. Hence, its probabilities were numerically mis-calibrated but directionally correct. All proofs have been formalized in Lean, thereby verifying correctness, and have been run through a semantic equivalence pipeline to ensure semantic equivalence between the formalized and informal statements. These are exploratory campaign outcomes, not fixed-budget success probabilities. The certificates prove formal statements; for a couple of questions, some geometric inputs are assumed in the lean proofs.

title: Hidden Sensitivity in LLM Pre-training: A Dynamic System View
justification: Sensitivity in LLM pre-training dynamics; training not inference.
hype_justification: Interesting dynamical-systems framing, moderate interest.
abstract: In Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, loss curves can conceal substantial instability, i.e., even small perturbations may lead to dramatically different predictions while leaving loss nearly unchanged. To investigate this phenomenon and reveal the underlying mechanisms, we first formulate LLM pre-training as a non-autonomous dynamical system that jointly evolves model weights and Adam optimizer states. Based on this formulation, we introduce a normalized sensitivity score in optimizer-relative coordinates to identify sensitive training checkpoints. At one such checkpoint, a weight perturbation of only 10^(-5) leads to 35.7% disagreement in top-1 predictions and 16.2% disagreement in benchmark answers after 200 training steps, with only 0.8% of greedy generations remaining identical despite similar validation losses. Furthermore, we find that perturbations to Adam's first and second moments induce comparably large effects, with similar sensitivity patterns observed in OLMo-1B. Finally, guided by our diagnostic, targeted stabilization reduces top-1 disagreement to 0.83% and increases generation exact match to 88.3%, at the cost of a 0.11-nat increase in validation loss. Our findings reveal a hidden form of optimizer-state-dependent sensitivity in LLM pre-training that conventional loss-based evaluations may overlook, while demonstrating its potential for diagnosis and mitigation.

title: Self-WSP: Can Language Models Improve Themselves Through Weight-Space Programming?
justification: Self weight-space programming for self-improvement; not an inference system.
hype_justification: RSI framing is a hot, hype-prone topic likely to draw clicks.
abstract: Frontier language models can now read and edit the weights of a neural network much like code and thereby improve a small model, an approach known as Weight-Space Programming (WSP). We further explore applying WSP to a language model itself, which we call Self-WSP. Specifically, Qwen3.5-0.8B reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and then continues with the edited weights as both problem solver and editor. We find many cases of genuine self-improvement. Self-edits can raise GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%, sometimes by changing only 16 parameters, and in some cases repeated self-editing keeps improving the model. A closer look, however, reveals that these gains lack interpretability. The model shows little understanding of the edits it makes, and WSP driven by random search sometimes performs comparably. Self-WSP thus holds promise as a path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), but realizing this promise requires further exploration.

title: Operational Assurance for LLM-Based Systems under Governance Opacity
justification: Governance/assurance framework for LLM services; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Conceptual governance proposal, niche audience.
abstract: In the contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem, foundation models are increasingly deployed under AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS) schemes characterized by high technical opacity, technological concentration, and limited external auditing capability over governance, training, and internal operational processes. Under these conditions, traditional ethical oversight approaches that focus exclusively on corporate governance or on internal model inspection become insufficient to ensure effective control over AI systems deployed in real-world contexts. This work proposes a pragmatic operational assurance framework inspired by Zero-Trust principles from cybersecurity, which shifts effective auditing efforts toward the application layer, where risk acquires observable, contextualized, and operationally verifiable properties. The proposal articulates two complementary evaluation levels: a black-box evaluation aimed at characterizing general behaviors, vulnerabilities, and risky capabilities of foundation models through conversational scanning, and a grey-box evaluation focused on the operational contextualization of risk within the actual deployment environment of the audited application. The framework incorporates mechanisms to move from general, CVSS-inspired severity metrics toward contextualized operational risk assessments that take into account user profiles, industrial domains, and organizational knowledge. In addition, the proposal strengthens practical auditability through digitally signed explainability reports (signed XAI reports), designed to support verifiable traceability, continuous monitoring, and operational accountability in LLM-based sociotechnical systems.

title: Learning How a Body Moves: Few-Shot Body Inference for Visual World Models of Animated Characters
justification: Few-shot body inference for animated-character world models; vision, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Novel benchmark but narrow niche.
abstract: Two visually identical animated characters can respond differently to the same action command because their body dynamics differ. For example, a stiff blob and its bouncy twin reach different heights when both receive the jump command. Given only the first frame and the action command, a visual world model has no information to distinguish these twins, because their initial appearances are identical. We therefore propose an in-context world model that encodes clips of a character's other actions into a body representation, using a contrastive loss to separate look-alike characters. We introduce ToonTwins, a benchmark of 144 2D cartoon characters that run, jump, fall, turn and crouch. Its characters form look-alike groups of four that differ only in their dynamics profile, and we also evaluate the model on 32 animated animals from DeformingThings4D. Even with a body code from these clips, the latent pixel world model we tested recovered at most 25 percent of the twins' jump height difference. On new shapes, our model identified the correct twin in 85.9 percent of cases, compared with 76.7 percent for a transformer baseline that reads the same clips without a body summary, and in a controlled ablation the contrastive loss gave more than half of this gain. On the animated animals, it reduced the mean path prediction error by 8.5 percent against a model without body information.

title: AgriManager: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-RL Generalization in Agricultural Management
justification: LLM-RL for agricultural management generalization; application, not inference.
hype_justification: Domain-specific framework, limited broad appeal.
abstract: Agricultural management is heterogeneous along two axes. The first is distributional shift within a fixed task interface: weather, crops, and prices vary across years and locations while sensors, actions, and objective stay fixed. The second is structural shift across interfaces: different farms expose different observed variables, available actions, and management objectives. We formalize the second axis as schema shift: variation in the policy-facing schema $Σ= (Σ_O, Σ_A, Σ_R)$ between training and deployment. We test whether LLM-RL generalizes across both axes with AgriManager, to our knowledge the first framework that trains LLM policies with RL across multiple process-based crop simulators, unifying DSSAT, WOFOST, and Cycles. We design a three-tier generalization ladder: Tier 1 within-schema distributional shift, Tier 2 single-axis schema shift along $Σ_O / Σ_A / Σ_R$, Tier 3 compositional schema shift across simulators, all scored on a frozen held-out test suite with three training seeds per method. Within fixed schemas, Qwen3-4B trained by RL with explicit reasoning exceeds neural-network PPO trained with the same interaction budget; without reasoning, training stalls near no-action where the reward penalizes input use. Under single-axis schema shift, $Σ_O$ transfer needs decision-critical state, $Σ_A$ results are consistent with joint action-menu coverage, and with reasoning a policy trained on yield alone transfers to unseen objectives. Under compositional schema shift, single-source training mostly hurts zero-shot transfer across simulators, and a unified policy trained only on other combinations of the same components recovers about 86% of the gain of a specialist trained on the target combination on DSSAT and stays below the specialists on the WOFOST and Cycles profit targets. Project page: https://agrimanager-framework.github.io

title: Bias Cascade: Understanding the Gap Between Knowledge Alignment and Effect Replication in LLM-based Social Simulation
justification: LLM social simulation benchmark; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Social-simulation benchmark, moderate niche interest.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate participants in social experiments. Existing research has primarily focused on aligning social knowledge and isolated responses, while overlooking whether simulations can reproduce the collective effects of social interventions. This distinction is critical due to a failure mechanism we call a $bias$ $cascade$: similar individual states can lead to different actions, while agreement on isolated actions can still produce divergent outcomes through dynamic interactions. As a result, models may produce accurate social judgments yet fail to reproduce the outcomes of classic human studies. To investigate this problem empirically, we introduce $REFLEX$ (Reproducing Effects of Foundational Literature EXperiments), a benchmark of 30 counterfactual social experiments grounded in classic human studies that compares knowledge judgment with effect simulation. Knowledge judgment directly predicts the direction of an intervention's effect, whereas effect simulation fixes the scenario and participants while varying one prespecified social factor, with agents generating actions from local observations that are aggregated into macro-level average treatment effects. Compared with human-study findings, the best-performing model achieves net directional scores of 0.847 for knowledge judgment and 0.453 for effect simulation. Moreover, longer causal chains are associated with poorer effect replication, consistent with the bias-cascade hypothesis. These findings reveal a substantial gap between knowledge alignment and effect replication, showing that current methods remain inadequate for reliably simulating collective human behavior.

title: Dynamic Model Merging with Multi-Layer Aggregated Routing Evidence
justification: Dynamic model merging routing on vision benchmarks; not LLM serving.
hype_justification: Incremental merging method on vision, niche.
abstract: Dynamic model merging aims to retain the efficiency of a unified model while better preserving task-specific expertise through input-dependent routing at both the task and head levels. However, even the routing components of the state-of-the-art approach remain limited: the task routing is highly sensitive to the choice of routing layer, whereas the head routing relies on simple max-logit competition. To address these limitations, we propose multi-layer aggregated routing evidence (MATE) as a unified mechanism for improving both task and head routing. Specifically, we first introduce a metric to quantify task routing separability across different layers. Empirical analysis of this metric reveals that different layers provide complementary evidence for identifying the tasks relevant to an input. Motivated by this observation, MATE selects multiple informative layers according to their routing separability and aggregates their layer-wise routing scores to produce a more robust signal that can be directly used for task selection. Moreover, we observe that this signal also encodes useful information about the suitability of the corresponding classification heads. This motivates us to further combine the MATE signal with the max-logit score to guide classification head selection. Extensive experiments on vision benchmarks demonstrate that MATE consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Thakaa at AlexandriaX-2026: Who Gets the Final Say? Assigning Output Authority in Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation and Error Detection
justification: Dialectal Arabic MT shared-task systems; NLP application, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Shared-task report, limited broad interest.
abstract: We report first-place systems for all four evaluated AlexandriaX-2026 settings: both English-to-dialect translation tracks, cross-dialect translation, and translation-error detection. In unconstrained translation, our minimum Bayes risk (MBR) selection restricts output authority: four local systems can supply the translation, while seven additional systems contribute only reference evidence. Candidate-constrained MBR beats the strongest complete candidate in all 13 dialects and gains 1.2554 macro spBLEU overall, reaching 33.4891. It also surpasses a retrospective oracle selecting the best whole candidate system per dialect. In the constrained track, country-routed LoRA adapters over a shared NileChat-3B-Base backbone incorporate the released Libyan and Sudanese supervision absent from the training and development splits, raising macro spBLEU from 29.5969 to 30.4233. Post-evaluation, a single adapter trained on all released Alexandria data reaches 30.4733 macro spBLEU; averaging model weights across three training seeds raises this to 30.9726 while retaining one model for inference. For cross-dialect translation, nonparallel target-dialect retrieval guides deliberation, raising Gemma-4-31B-IT without fine-tuning from 24.6898 to 28.4011 spBLEU. For translation-error detection, GPT-5.5 proposes semantic error regions, while MARBERTv2 controls their character boundaries and corroborates additional spans, raising Overall from 0.4691 to 0.4982.

title: Interaction Retention and Output-Likelihood Training in Parallel Sampling
justification: Theory of parallel sampling distortion in masked diffusion LMs; touches generation but mostly theoretical.
hype_justification: Dense theory, limited accessibility despite diffusion-LM relevance.
abstract: Parallel samplers such as masked diffusion language models generate several coordinates per step from conditional marginals and randomize which coordinates are generated together, so even exact conditionals return a distorted distribution. We give an exact local account of this distortion. Around any full-support product law, the Gram operator of the sampler's response is diagonal in the interaction decomposition, and its eigenvalues are retention probabilities: the probability that an interaction has a unique latest-revealed coordinate. This retention spectrum determines the exact frontier between output accuracy and conditional calibration, its regularization path, and the population response of finite-mixture likelihood training. For pairwise interactions it yields a sharp dichotomy. Under homogeneous retention, output-likelihood training is equivalent to a single context gain; heterogeneous retention opens correction directions beyond any scalar, with an advantage bounded by an explicit heterogeneity gap. On binarized digits and MNIST, output-likelihood training within a heterogeneous schedule library lowers calibrated test negative log-likelihood in all twelve paired comparisons, and the gain survives pair-specific recalibration and a stronger path optimizer. For a frozen 169.6-million-parameter masked diffusion language model, serially normalized context gains are 1.070 and 1.056 at 8 and 16 rounds, against the predicted values 1.134 and 1.058.

title: Thakaa at StanceEval-2026: Inference-Time Target Grounding for Arabic Stance Detection
justification: Inference-time target grounding for Arabic stance detection; NLP task, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Shared-task system paper, niche.
abstract: StanceEval-2026 tests Arabic stance classification under target shift, with evaluation targets absent from the labelled task data. We test two ways to supply target information at inference time. For Track 1, we retrieve eight labelled Women Driving demonstrations from the external ArabicStanceX corpus and score the three label tokens with Gemma-4-31B-IT. For the unseen-target track, we prepend cached target context prompted to be factual and non-evaluative, then fuse label predictions and label-token scores from multiple LLMs, with final assignments constrained by published class totals. The systems obtain 85.22 and 91.78 Favg2 on Tracks 1 and 2, ranking sixth and fourth in the final standings. On held-out ArabicStanceX tweets, direct prompting scores 79.45 Favg2; eight random Women Driving demonstrations raise it to 84.78, and similarity retrieval reaches 89.04. Across three target-held-out Mawqif evaluations, a fixed target card raises Gemma-4-31B-IT from 86.54 to 86.93, whereas QLoRA lowers Gemma-4-12B-IT from 84.43 to 83.77. In these separate public evaluations, same-target demonstrations and retrieval improve performance, factual target context provides small, target-dependent gains, and the tested source-only adapter does not improve.

title: KineState-SWAM: A Surgical World Action Model with Explicit Kinematics and Causal Interaction Dynamics
justification: Surgical world-action model; robotics/video, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Domain-specific with dataset, limited appeal.
abstract: Existing surgical world models often leave implicit how instrument motion drives localized tissue responses and how interaction history informs subsequent actions. We introduce KineState-SWAM, a surgical world-action model coupling action prediction and video generation through a persistent interaction state, separating kinematically determined instrument motion from learned scene evolution. A flow-matching policy predicts joint trajectories conditioned on interaction state, robot configuration, and task instruction. Kinematic Geometry Conditioning converts these trajectories into surface-motion tokens and spatially aligned instrument renderings using calibrated URDF kinematics. Causal Interaction Dynamics recurrently updates the state through geometry-guided attention and motion-aligned feature transport, carrying interaction history into subsequent action predictions without intermediate video synthesis. The State-Geometry Adapter combines state-dependent spatial modulation with localized geometric residuals to guide video generation. Interaction-aware supervision emphasizes tissue responses near instrument working regions. We introduce dVRK-Chole5.2k, comprising 5,255 videos spanning 17 surgical tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines within matched action-conditioning settings. Ablations support preserving and transporting interaction states for long-horizon prediction.

title: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
justification: Action tokenizer for robot policies; touches inference latency but focus is VLA control.
hype_justification: Scaling across embodiments is trendy in robotics-foundation-model space.
abstract: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.

title: Correlation-aware sequential sampling for multi-output polynomial chaos expansions
justification: Sampling for polynomial chaos expansions; UQ surrogate modeling, unrelated.
hype_justification: Highly specialized numerical-methods topic.
abstract: The interaction of multiple physical processes in complex engineering systems is often characterized by several quantities of interest (QoIs) with non-negligible cross-correlations. Accurate uncertainty quantification of these responses requires repeated model evaluations, which can be computationally expensive. As an alternative, polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) provides an efficient surrogate modeling framework for reducing this computational cost owing to its natural structure for statistical analysis, while adaptive sequential sampling can further improve sampling efficiency under a limited model evaluation budget. However, adaptive sampling strategies specifically designed for multi-output PCE remain limited, and existing approaches commonly aggregate information from individual outputs without explicitly accounting for their statistical dependence. When strong correlations exist among QoIs, output-wise aggregation can give greater combined influence to response patterns shared by several outputs. To reduce the influence of such repeated representation on sample allocation, this study develops a principal component analysis-based extension of the multi-output criterion for adaptive construction of PCE. The sampling criterion combines component-wise normalization with the retention of selected principal directions, thereby adjusting the relative influence of shared response patterns while preserving distance-based exploration. The method is verified through numerical examples with different levels of output coupling and is compared with the conventional multi-output criterion and reference sampling strategies. The results demonstrate that accounting for output dependence improves the allocation of new samples among multiple response features and enhances the efficiency of multi-output PCE surrogate construction, particularly for strongly correlated QoIs.

title: FormaFin: Verifiable Financial Analysis with Solver-Guided Reinforcement Learning
justification: Training small models to formalize financial rules; application, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Practical fintech angle, moderate niche interest.
abstract: Formally verifying financial analyses generated by large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as financial rules are largely expressed in natural language and rarely have corresponding formal specifications. Training language models to formalize these rules is hindered by the scarcity of labeled data and reliable training signals, while confidential financial data favor small models that run locally. We introduce FormaFin, a framework that trains small open language models to translate financial rules into reusable SMT formulas. FormaFin integrates teacher distillation with reinforcement learning using an SMT solver to compute rewards from numerical thresholds stated in financial rules. We evaluate FormaFin on corporate loan monitoring, in which lenders check borrowers' financial figures against loan agreements. To evaluate our framework, we curate \bench{}, a benchmark containing 143 loan agreements and 2,527 questions covering compliance, earnings cushion, and debt capacity. Our results show that a 7B formalizer achieves 94.8\% accuracy, outperforming open LLMs up to ten times larger. Across three model families, accuracy ranges from 92.6 to 96.8\%. Our framework also detects 95.6 to 99.7\% of errors in other LLMs' financial analyses. We make FormaFin and \bench{} publicly available.

title: Refined, Reliable and Reproducible: Algorithmic Analysis and Reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder
justification: Cosmic void finder reimplementation; astrophysics, unrelated.
hype_justification: Astro software paper, no ML-inference audience.
abstract: Cosmic voids are vast underdense regions of the Universe that encode valuable information about its large-scale structure and evolution. By extending spherical voids into overlapping sphere structures, the Popcorn Void Finder demonstrated an improved statistical characterization of cosmic void populations. However, its origin as a research prototype progressively hindered its maintainability and extensibility. Moreover, post-publication algorithmic modifications have not been systematically evaluated, leaving their statistical and computational consequences insufficiently characterized. In this work, we present a comprehensive reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder, prioritizing algorithmic transparency, maintainability, and reproducibility. We document the complete identification procedure, revisit the original algorithmic choices, and evaluate their statistical and computational consequences. Comparisons between implementations revealed a significant change in the behavior of the Void Size Function, which is now characterized by a power-law regime transitioning to a Schechter-like distribution. These changes not only provide a better characterization of void sizes, but enable a new and more robust method to the determination of the shot-noise dominated regime, without implicit dependencies on internal finder parameters present in previous works. Performance benchmarks demonstrate a 1.62x speedup in spherical void identification and a substantial improvement in overlap-removal throughput. We determined the Popcorn algorithm to be negatively affected by load imbalance, and found a speedup of 63x in a tested configuration with a newly introduced early growth termination criterion. These results establish a more maintainable and reproducible foundation for popcorn void identification, while clarifying the statistical and computational trade-offs that govern its performance.

title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation
justification: Agentic MLLM audiovisual-creation benchmark; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Creative-agent benchmark, some interest in video-gen community.
abstract: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.

title: STRIDE: Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-Guided Skill Disclosure and Evolution for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
justification: Skill-augmented agentic RL framework; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Agentic RL is trendy but this is incremental.
abstract: Skill-augmented reinforcement learning enables LLM agents to reuse task-solving knowledge across episodes, but existing systems typically expose agents to a flat skill pool and update skills only from coarse, episode-level outcomes. This conflates two distinct uses of experience: a stable strategy that should frame the whole episode, and tactical know-how that should be retrieved only when the agent reaches a local execution gap. We propose STRIDE (Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-guided skIll Disclosure and Evolution), a framework that brings progressive skill disclosure into agentic reinforcement learning. STRIDE keeps the selected strategy visible as episode context, exposes a compact tactic menu, and loads full tactic content only after an explicit retrieval action. This interface turns each retrieval into an event-level credit unit: the same event provides process feedback for learning when to retrieve and supplies evidence for skill-bank evolution. On ALFWorld, STRIDE achieves a 92.7% average success rate with Qwen3-4B and a 94.9% average success rate with Qwen3-8B. On WebShop, it improves over the strongest reproduced skill-augmented baseline by 4.5 score points and 1.9 success-rate percentage points. These results show that skill reuse is most effective when persistent strategies preserve global task structure and tactics are disclosed only at local decision bottlenecks.

title: Can Open LLMs Clear Sanctions-Screening Alerts? A Pre-registered Test on Public Sanctions Lists with Turkish Name Variants
justification: Open LLMs for sanctions screening on-prem; deployment application, not inference optimization.
hype_justification: Pre-registered fintech evaluation, niche.
abstract: Sanctions screening raises name-based alerts that are mostly false positives, and level-1 analysts clear them by checking the customer's date of birth and name against a written policy. We test whether open-weight language models that a bank can run on its own premises can perform this level-1 disposition. From the UK and EU sanctions lists (7,103 natural persons) we built 12,200 synthetic customers: listed persons under six name conditions, including Turkish spellings of Arabic-origin names and Turkish romanisations of Cyrillic names, and two date-of-birth conditions, plus namesakes, near-name customers and a general population. A deterministic fuzzy and embedding screen raised 7,383 alerts, which three open models served on domestic infrastructure and three rule baselines dispositioned under the same policy. The models sent far fewer innocent customers to level 2 than a rule that applies the policy's date clause: 0.6 to 16.9 per 1,000 screened customers against 24.4, and they stated the date-of-birth status correctly in 98.3% to 98.5% of alerts. They also failed to escalate 1.5% to 2.2% of the listed persons. The pre-registered non-inferiority test against the rule was met, but only because of a construction error we found after the analysis: 21 customers in the "minor discrepancy" condition had dates that conflict under the policy. Without them the rule misses no listed person and no model meets the margin. The misses had model-specific causes: one model read minor date discrepancies as conflicts, one declared word-order and typing variants to be different names, and one discounted alerts that its own rationale said to escalate. Fuzzy matching found 69% of the Turkish spellings of Arabic-origin names; adding embeddings raised this to 74%. Open LLMs can cut level-1 workload, but on this evidence only behind a deterministic date check and with every name doubt escalated.

title: Definition-Guided In-Context Learning for Zero-Shot Spoken Language Understanding
justification: Definition-guided ICL for zero-shot SLU; speech NLP method, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Incremental speech-understanding method, niche.
abstract: Adapting spoken language understanding (SLU) systems to novel or revised label taxonomies conventionally requires additional labeled data and retraining, creating a bottleneck for real world deployment. While in-context learning with few-shot demonstrations offers an alternative, multi-modal generalization and scaling has been challenging. In this work, we investigate whether natural-language definitions alone can guide zero-shot SLU without demonstration exemplars, finding that symbolic definitions serve as the primary supervisory driver for adapting speech-text models. We operationalize this principle as Definition-Guided In-Context Learning (DG-ICL), a fine-tuning framework that decouples semantic categories from fixed lexical names. By replacing labels with dynamically randomized definitions (arbitrary synthetic tokens in DG-ICL-Sym or permuted vocabulary words in DG-ICL-Flip), DG-ICL avoids lexical shortcuts and encourages the model to ground acoustic representations in contextual definitions. Novel categories can thus be introduced at inference simply by defining them through the instructions. Across three speech-text models (AUDIO FLAMINGO 3, QWEN2-AUDIO, and SALMONN), DG-ICL outperforms standard instruction tuning on held-out tasks under novel symbols (0.663 vs. 0.449 macro-F1 on Audio Flamingo 3; 0.703 vs. 0.620 on Qwen2-Audio; 0.582 vs. 0.399 on SALMONN), while remaining competitive on original labels. Furthermore, counterfactual evaluations demonstrate instruction following abilities, where it is shown that DG-ICL-Sym retains 68% of its performance when definitions contradict pre-trained lexical priors, whereas standard instruction tuning elicits significantly reduced retention of 21%. Finally, we show that DG-ICL enables zero-shot speech clustering into user-defined categories specified on the fly

title: STEdgeFormer: MCU and NPU Deployable Transformer Architecture
justification: Hardware-aware transformer for MCU/NPU deployment; genuinely about inference latency/operator constraints though small-scale.
hype_justification: Edge-deployment focus, single author, modest reach.
abstract: Transformer-based sequence models have achieved strong performance in language and time-series modeling, but self-attention remains computationally and memory intensive for deployment on resource-constrained edge accelerators. We propose STEdgeFormer, a lightweight, hardware-aware sequence architecture designed for efficient execution on embedded neural accelerators. STEdgeFormer combines polynomial mixture layers and DyT normalization with an accelerator-aware causal memory block, replacing pairwise self-attention with compact causal aggregation. On TinyStories, the fully NPU-supported STEdgeFormer (MW) achieves a perplexity of 7.39 with 4.12M parameters and 6.51 MB RAM, with an end-to-end latency of 40 ms. In comparison, the standard 4.12M-parameter configuration achieves a lower perplexity of 6.79 but requires CPU fallback for unsupported operators, resulting in 1450 ms latency. Vanilla Transformer, on the other hand, achieves a perplexity score of 5.71 using a 4.40M-parameter model, but it cannot be deployed on the hardware. On downstream tasks, STEdgeFormer achieves 94% accuracy on ECG5000 and 93% accuracy on Speech Commands with 1.39M parameters. These results demonstrate that hardware-aware architectural choices and operator compatibility can have a substantial impact on practical inference latency, beyond model size and task accuracy alone. Rather than targeting state-of-the-art accuracy on individual benchmarks, STEdgeFormer is designed to provide a deployable sequence modeling architecture under the memory, computational, and operator constraints of embedded neural accelerators.

title: When Rubrics Do Not Decide: Silent Value Completion in LLM Evaluation
justification: LLM-judge evaluation failure modes; evaluation, not inference systems.
hype_justification: LLM-judge reliability is topical, moderate interest.
abstract: Multi-criterion LLM judges often evaluate responses without specifying how conflicting criteria resolve, leaving the winner undetermined even under exact criterion scores. Issuing a strict verdict without declaring the required trade-off premise constitutes silent value completion. We introduce TradeoffBench to isolate this failure by separating rule execution from response scoring. On authoritative criterion vectors, six open-weight non-reasoning judges pass all dominance and equality controls yet pick unsupported winners on 9%-81% of 1,345 conflicts. All 577 order-stable choices follow an explicitly banned majority rule. Reasoning-enabled configurations drop anonymous-vector violations to 2 in 9,720 judgments under an explicit rule, yet cannot bridge omitted trade-offs or divergent component scoring. On raw TradeoffBench text with unspecified trade-offs, GPT-6.1-sol omits its completion premise in 29.8% of 400 verified conflicts. Even under an explicit rule on four-rater-consensus MultiPref conflicts, four reasoning judges still issue strict verdicts on 16/45 (GPT-6.1-sol) up to 35/46 and 25/29 (open-weight judges) of valid presentations. We propose identified-first evaluation, decoupling specification support, explicit completion, and target agreement. In MultiPref human-score audits, peer-mean substitution raises directional disagreement from 0.6% to 28.8% on 2,707 shared targets. A single-peer ablation confirms a 29.38-point gap on 2,175 targets, ruling out averaging as the cause. In HUMAINE, declared partial trade-offs add 2.5 percentage points of coverage, yet newly decided pairs incur 3.9% disagreement versus 0.9% for Pareto. Reliable LLM judging, therefore, requires auditing, specification support, declared trade-offs, and human target agreement separately.

title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
justification: Proactive perception for computer-use agents; reduces VLM inference latency/stale actions, partly inference-efficiency.
hype_justification: Computer-use agents are hot and the latency angle is practical.
abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than $30\times$ its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.

title: Micro Operational Robustness of LLMs on Code Generation
justification: Robustness of LLM code generation to prompt variation; evaluation, not inference.
hype_justification: Uses dated models, limited appeal.
abstract: It is now common practice in software development for large language models (LLMs) to be used to generate program code. It is desirable to evaluate the robustness of LLMs for this usage. This paper is concerned in particular with how sensitive LLMs are to variations in descriptions of the coding tasks. However, existing techniques for evaluating this robustness are unsuitable for code generation because the input data space of natural language (NL) descriptions is discrete and sparse. To address this problem, we propose a robustness evaluation method called scenario domain analysis, which aims to find the expected minimal change in the NL descriptions of coding tasks that would cause the LLMs to produce incorrect outputs. We have formally proved the theoretical properties of the method and also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of four state-of-the-art LLMs: Gemini-pro, Codex, Llamma2 and Falcon 7B, and have found that we are able to rank these with confidence from best to worst. Moreover, we have also studied how robustness varies in different scenarios, including the variations with the topic of the coding task and with the complexity of its sample solution, and found that robustness is lower for more complex tasks and also lower for more advanced topics, such as multi-threading and data structures.

title: EmoRouter: Adaptive Modality Cascading for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
justification: Adaptive modality cascading cuts inference latency for Omni-LLM emotion recognition; inference efficiency but domain-specific.
hype_justification: Training-free efficiency method with code, moderate interest.
abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) involves detecting the underlying emotion behind each utterance within a conversation, which is essential for emotionally aware human-computer interaction. While omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) demonstrate strong capability for MER by jointly processing modalities including text, audio, and vision, different modality combinations yield different prediction outcomes across utterances: acoustic and visual inputs can help recover annotated labels missed by text-only inference, but can also turn correct predictions into errors. Processing all modalities for every utterance is also computationally expensive. To this end, we introduce EmoRouter, a training-free, model-agnostic framework for adaptive modality cascading that selects an exit tier for each utterance along a predefined modality order. The routing is guided by prediction-uncertainty estimates derived from Conformal Prediction. EmoRouter routes each utterance through a sequence of increasing-cost modality levels and exits at the first level when the model is confident in the emotion. To determine when to exit, we propose Conformal Set Contraction, a structural calibration criterion that calibrates the per-tier CP error budgets used for these exit decisions. Comprehensive evaluations on 4 MER benchmarks and 3 Omni-LLMs reveal that EmoRouter matches or outperforms the full modalities while reducing inference latency by 67.9--94.5%. Furthermore, EmoRouter demonstrates high transferability across different models, validating its robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi-lab/EmoRouter.

title: Learning Land-Surface Hydrology World Model from Satellite Observations
justification: Land-surface hydrology world model from satellites; geoscience, unrelated.
hype_justification: Earth-science ML, no inference audience.
abstract: A world model should tell us not only what will happen, but what would happen under a different action. Learned Earth models now forecast remarkably well, yet forecast skill says little about what their state means or how it responds to a changed driver. We build LandWM, a world model of land-surface water in which rain is the action, learned from seven years of SMAP and CYGNSS observations: physical observation operators tie its latent state to soil water, and a mass-conserving balance governs how that state responds to rain. Over the U.S. Southern Great Plains, the model, never shown a soil-moisture value, tracks 28 in-situ probes as well as the operational SMAP Level-4 product, even from CYGNSS alone, and a storm added to the forcing of a station's cell wets its soil as natural storms wet the probes. Replace either piece and the forecasts stay, but the meaning goes: with neural operators, only a probe fitted to the stations finds the soil water; with a generic recurrent transition, rain on a single cell barely moves it. Yet when the same rain covers the whole region the two transitions swap roles, and the conserving one responds too weakly. Grounding makes a world model readable; its response to actions must be tested under more than one kind of intervention.

title: MolReJev: Decision Models Are In-Context Molecular Predictors
justification: In-context molecular prediction; mentions inference cost/throughput but focus is molecular ML.
hype_justification: Niche molecular-ML with throughput claims.
abstract: Molecular prediction helps prioritize compounds for screening. Specialized predictors are trained for a fixed set of tasks, limiting cross-task generalization. Language models can condition on task descriptions and have recently shown promise in molecular prediction. However, generating answers token by token adds inference cost, and general-purpose models often lack task-specific molecular knowledge. We thus propose MolReJev, which combines Jev-style candidate scoring with in-context learning (ICL) on a language model. MolReJev retrieves similar labeled examples from existing task data and scores candidate labels jointly in one forward pass. ICL improves predictions from the released general-purpose Kev checkpoint and the separately trained MolReJev. For the trained model, gains span all evaluation groups, including held-out tasks, and extend to compounds absent from training. MolReJev generally outperforms MolecularGPT on matched evaluations and nearest-neighbor prediction with the same examples. With four examples, MolReJev and a trained text baseline achieve similar ROC-AUC, with higher measured throughput for MolReJev. These results show that decision models can serve as in-context molecular predictors for compounds, drug pairs, and reactions.

title: A Design Space for Data Agents: Insights from KDD Cup 2026
justification: Design-space analysis of data agents from a competition; not inference systems.
hype_justification: KDD Cup retrospective, moderate niche interest.
abstract: Data agents interpret analytical requests, gather evidence from heterogeneous sources, and compute results within finite resource budgets. We analyze the final code submissions of the ten highest-ranked teams in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents for Complex Data Analysis competition. We organize the observed design choices into three interacting layers, covering workflow orchestration, analytical functions, and working state. The comparison reveals recurring patterns for allocating computation in response to task progress, structuring evidence for computation and assessment, and preserving reusable artifacts with their provenance. Candidates that rely on the same evidence can inherit the same error, so interpreting their agreement requires tracing those dependencies. The design space motivates controlled evaluations of how resource allocation, evidence sharing, and targeted recovery affect task completion and correctness.

title: When Wrong Answers Remain Unsettled: Failure Dynamics in Recurrent Reasoners
justification: Failure dynamics in recurrent reasoners (HRM/TRM); touches inference-time compute but interpretability-focused.
hype_justification: HRM/TRM are trendy; careful analysis may draw some attention.
abstract: When a recurrent reasoner returns a wrong answer, is its computation finished or merely stopped? We test this on a trained Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM; 27M parameters, Sudoku-Extreme) by running the recurrence for one more inference budget and comparing with an unperturbed control. Solved answers persist (0.95 of 512 endpoints). Wrong answers mostly do not: 0.42 of near-miss answers (n=170) and 0.18 of all 512 wrong endpoints keep their answer. Perturbations from 0.05x to 20x the terminal-update scale barely change these rates, so the measurement reflects continued recurrence, not noise sensitivity. The solved-above-wrong ordering also holds in five further settings (a second seed, TRM, Maze, GRAM-guided TRM, N-Queens), but a fixed 1/2 persistence threshold does not, and neither do HRM's endpoint-spectrum and fast-versus-slow predictability patterns, which are not universal diagnostics. Perturb-and-reselect (known from prior work) is consistent with this: frozen noise gains 4.8 accuracy points (197 gained, 2 lost), but compute-matched extended depth gains 5.6 and Sudoku symmetry augmentation 34.6, so noise is not the best use of the budget. Conclusions are limited to finite horizons and one primary HRM checkpoint; they do not exclude asymptotic attractors.

title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
justification: Rotation-based test-time training for MLLMs; inference-time adaptation but not serving/optimization.
hype_justification: Simple TTT method, moderate interest.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.

title: CLASP: Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling for Zero-Shot OOD Detection using Vision-Language Models
justification: Zero-shot OOD detection with medical VLMs; not inference systems.
hype_justification: Medical-imaging OOD, niche.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in medical imaging, yet existing approaches often rely on final-layer confidence or entropy-based layer selection, potentially missing complementary information. We show that low in-distribution (ID) confidence entropy does not reliably predict OOD discrimination. We introduce CLASP (Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling), an ID-only framework that jointly models layer--prompt responses and visual features. CLASP ranks visual encoder layers using Gaussian conditional mutual information and selects a compact subset through anchored spectral selection, without fixing the number of layers. It then combines the selected layer--prompt profiles with PCA-compressed visual embeddings and fits a single shrinkage-regularized Gaussian. OOD scores are computed using squared Mahalanobis distance, without fine-tuning, OOD training data, or test-time adaptation. Across histopathology, chest X-ray, and brain MRI benchmarks with UniMedCLIP and BioMedCLIP, CLASP performs strongly under varied distribution shifts. On MIDOG near-OOD, it achieves 87.54% AUROC with UniMedCLIP, outperforming confidence-based baselines; with BioMedCLIP, it remains competitive but trails visual-only Mahalanobis modeling. Ablations highlight the value of layer--prompt interactions and cross-feature dependencies, while exposing shift-dependent contributions and limitations under semantic shifts.

title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
justification: Supervised long-context multi-step retriever for RAG; retrieval component, tangential to inference systems.
hype_justification: Cheap long-context retriever is practical and may get adoption.
abstract: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.

title: Elicitation format changes zero-shot classification accuracy in a medical vision-language model: a two-center evaluation on colorectal histopathology
justification: Elicitation-format effects in a medical VLM; evaluation, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Careful two-center study, niche clinical-ML audience.
abstract: Background. Verbalized confidence from a hosted medical vision-language model is usually treated as packaging around an unchanged prediction. Methods. We held a nine-class colorectal histopathology prompt fixed except for the requested response format and evaluated MedGemma-27b-it on 10,004 validation and 7,180 external-center PathMNIST patches, with preregistered endpoints, randomized ties, and random floors recomputed for each patch set. Results. Requesting probabilities over all nine classes instead of a ranked top-3 reduced accuracy by 14.8 points on validation, -0.1475 [-0.1594, -0.1353], and 13.4 at the external center, -0.1341 [-0.1484, -0.1196], against chance accuracy of 0.1111. The nine-class prompt uniquely forbade commentary, reasoning, and a chosen answer; removing that prohibition at matched cardinality and token budget recovered +0.1878 [+0.1623, +0.2134] and +0.1911 [+0.1648, +0.2181], while changing cardinality with the prohibition absent moved accuracy by -0.0013 [-0.0300, +0.0280] and -0.0214 [-0.0494, +0.0071].
