title: From Head to Tail: LLM-Augmented Sequential Recommendation and Trade-off Optimization
justification: LLM-augmented recommendation, not inference systems.
hype_justification: RecSys with LLM augmentation, moderate.
abstract: Recommender systems exhibit popularity bias, often under-serving long-tail and cold-start items with sparse interaction data. We propose a group-specific data augmentation approach that leverages LLMs to generate synthetic interactions, formulated as a constrained optimization problem, maximizing group-specific NDCG@20 and coverage while bounding overall NDCG@20 degradation within an acceptable threshold. Items are partitioned by interaction frequency to find the optimal augmentation strategy for each group. We further study combining the augmentation across groups simultaneously and find that while individual optimal strategies navigate the multi-group augmentation design, they are not simply additive. We further ablate on the LLM-based augmentation itself, comparing LLM scales, augmentation configuration under token constraints, finding that augmentation quality scales with contextual richness, albeit at a proportionally higher cost. Experiments with SASRec demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving over 100% and 60% improvement in group-specific NDCG@20 for extreme and regular long-tail items, respectively, on our industrial dataset, and 40%, 25% for MovieLens-32M, while increasing their coverage without significant overall degradation.

title: DKnown-Jev-2: Article-Level Answer-Evidence Classification and Efficient Inference with a Pre-trained Language Model
justification: Article-level classifier with low-latency non-autoregressive inference; efficiency angle but narrow QA model.
hype_justification: Specialized normative QA model.
abstract: Evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering requires determining whether a candidate article contains content that directly supports an answer under the applicable conditions of the question. We present DKnown-Jev-2, an article-level answer evidence classifier designed for evidence integration across multiple paragraphs. The model jointly encodes question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, and uses a pointer-style classification head to predict Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE) in a single forward pass. Ona manually annotated test set of 972 evaluation instances, DKnown-Jev-2 achieves 91.77% accuracy and 91.28% macro-F1, outperforming Jev by 2.16 and 2.37 percentage points, respectively, while reducing both evidence misses and non-evidence false positives. The test set contains 317 multi-paragraph instances, with a maximum body length of 9,322 characters. Shared article encoding and non-autoregressive classification support low-latency inference. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for article-level evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering.

title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
justification: Multi-agent error propagation modeling, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Multi-agent reliability, topical but incremental.
abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning
justification: Hard-budget LLM reasoning with single-rollout conformal control; touches inference budget/cost but mainly reasoning reliability.
hype_justification: Budgeted reasoning is relevant; unknown authors.
abstract: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.

title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
justification: Circuit reconstruction agent benchmark, unrelated.
hype_justification: Hardware agent benchmark, niche.
abstract: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.

title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression
justification: Training-free residual-sign quantization for Transformer weight compression, directly inference-oriented.
hype_justification: LLM quantization is hot but novel scheme from less-known group, no code/codebooks.
abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
justification: LLM-discovered heuristics for vehicle routing, unrelated.
hype_justification: Combinatorial optimization niche.
abstract: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for selecting subproblems, enabling effective optimization of large-scale CVRP instances. Compared to prior approaches that train task-specific neural networks to select among heuristically constructed subproblems, our method discovers generalizable, interpretable LLM-generated heuristics to directly construct subproblems. Experiments show that our approach achieves comparable in-distribution performance while outperforming neural network-based policies on out-of-distribution instances with large-scale problems.

title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
justification: Human-AI task allocation behavioral study, unrelated.
hype_justification: Princeton/MIT authors, labor-AI topical; not technical.
abstract: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. As AI also makes decisions about work allocation, we compare a set of LLMs. We find many models also deviate from purely objective decisions, particularly when the project stakes are low, but there is wide heterogeneity as to how much and in what manner they weigh enjoyment. These results raise questions about what role human experience may play in decisions around where and how to integrate AI into workplaces. Integration may be jagged across settings due to consideration not only of the relative capabilities of workers, but also the human experience of work, the valence of that experience (e.g., more strongly weighing aversion), the context (e.g., stakes), and who is making or guiding such choices (human or LLM).

title: Leakage-Safe Auditing of Attribution-Driven Data Curation in Medical Imaging
justification: Medical imaging data curation auditing, unrelated.
hype_justification: Specialized medical imaging.
abstract: When can an attribution-derived anomaly justify changing a medical-imaging training set? We formulate attribution-driven curation as three separately testable claims: anomaly detection, harmfulness estimation, and intervention utility. We test the first and third using a patient-disjoint, identifier-preserving audit of a 3D convolutional classifier for computed tomography angiography aneurysm candidates. We identify 232 exactly zero-valued arrays among 1,201 positive patches, including 170 training positives, and invalidate a historical 321-patch attention-failure subgroup whose identifier-free records were joined to files by position. On the held-out test set, GradCAM++ spatial concentration is central for every candidate class, reversing the historical pattern. GradCAM++ and Integrated Gradients show negative rank-order agreement for positives, limiting method-independent anatomical interpretation. Across five paired training seeds, removing the 170 corrupted training positives yields AUC 0.9617 +/- 0.0044 versus 0.9652 +/- 0.0039 for full-data training (difference -0.0035; 95% CI -0.0082 to 0.0007). Excluding 34 raw-zero test positives widens rather than closes the gap, countering a blank-memorization explanation. Budget-matched random-removal controls suggest the result is not simply an effect of reducing training size. Input corruption does not necessarily imply that deletion improves generalization. Our framework makes leakage control, sample identity, and intervention testing explicit in attribution-driven medical-imaging data curation.

title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech
justification: Voice-agent early-speech controller; test-time control but not inference serving.
hype_justification: Voice agent latency novelty, moderate.
abstract: Speaking early turns a prediction into an irreversible public commitment. We introduce SayWhen, a test-time controller that selects a task-directed act shared across typed continuation plans and controls its release as speech. A persistent veto blocks playback when intervening transcripts invalidate the candidate. We define regret-free early speech (RFES) to measure supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility. On a 72-prefix branching diagnostic, the generated-plan frontier attains 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret, versus 8.2% RFES and 0.068 regret for Matched Top-One. Measured planner latency constrains this path; a deterministic retail schema attains 31.7% RFES, compared with 32.0% for the complete policy. In a separate 30-task $τ$-Voice simulation, schema-derived candidates with cached text-to-speech (TTS) audio attain 21/30 task-level RFES. Eligible audio begins 1.51 seconds before the user-audio endpoint among the 22 tasks with early speech, or 1.11 seconds over all 30 tasks with zero for tasks without eligible early speech. Semantic veto and endpoint waiting each pass 16/30 tasks. Together, the studies demonstrate a controlled coverage-compatibility trade-off and schema-based pre-endpoint operation, making the supported public commitment an explicit unit of voice-agent control.

title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
justification: Exact KV cache migration across LoRA updates for LLM agents, core inference serving topic.
hype_justification: KV cache + adapter serving is practical and hot; strong speedup claims, adoptable.
abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.

title: Look Back, Draft Ahead: Corrective Prefix Attention for Parallel Speculative Decoding
justification: Corrective prefix attention for parallel speculative decoding, directly inference acceleration.
hype_justification: Speculative decoding is a hot topic; strong speedups on NPUs, Huawei-affiliated team.
abstract: Parallel speculative decoders propose an entire token block at once, yet one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject its remaining suffix. We introduce Corrective Prefix Attention (CPA), which combines prefix-aware selection with autoregressive supervision to improve these parallel drafts. CPA lets each candidate attend to earlier choices within the block. Fixed candidate shortlists allow all pairwise interactions to be computed before selection, reducing the sequential walk to table lookups, accumulation and lightweight scoring rather than repeated neural evaluations. An auxiliary autoregressive loss trains the shared backbone on clean prefixes without adding an inference pass. Across eight math, code and dialogue benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B targets on Ascend NPUs, CPA commits 13--15\% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25--26\% more than DFlash. Its mean speedups reach $3.35\times$ and $3.37\times$ under greedy decoding and $2.86\times$ under sampling for both targets. Ablations support both components, while capacity sweeps demonstrate that greater acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding. These results motivate correcting parallel proposals with causal information while keeping sequential computation inexpensive.

title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
justification: Robot-use interface benchmark, not inference.
hype_justification: Embodied agent interface study, moderate.
abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
justification: Self-upgrading embodied agents via weight editing; lifelong learning not inference systems.
hype_justification: Bold recursive self-improvement claims likely to attract attention and debate.
abstract: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

title: TideSand: Performance-Accurate Sandbox Multiplexing for LLM Agents
justification: Sandbox resource multiplexing for performance-sensitive LLM agents, an inference-serving systems problem.
hype_justification: Berkeley group (Gonzalez, Cheung, Lee); practical agent-serving system likely to draw interest.
abstract: We propose TideSand, a sandbox system that intelligently multiplexes resources for performance-sensitive LLM agents, such as auto research agents working on system measurement tasks. TideSand combines three key ideas: agent-aware scheduling, which schedules sandbox execution intelligently at the tool call level to avoid resource contention; speculative swapping, which offloads the memory of sandboxes waiting on inference and restores it before their next tool call; and selective rollback, which checkpoints selected sandboxes when contention occurs and restores them when machines are idle. We evaluate TideSand across six model-workload pairs on AlgoTune, Terminal-Bench 4.0, and Terminal-Bench Science. TideSand achieves 3.8-10x higher throughput than strict reservation while maintaining tool-call fidelity, or 7-44% higher fidelity than overcommit baselines at similar throughput. Moreover, TideSand reduces the evaluation error on Algotune by 19x through improved tool-call fidelity. We hope the work motivates future research to maintain tool call fidelity while keeping resource utilization high through statistical multiplexing.

title: Site-Conditioned Boundary Closure for Subsurface Seepage Forecasting and Relief Placement
justification: Subsurface seepage forecasting, unrelated.
hype_justification: Geoscience modeling, niche.
abstract: Truncating a large heterogeneous diffusion model around a localized, threshold-activated outlet saves degrees of freedom but severs exterior feedback that governs when the outlet opens and how much it discharges. By separating forcing-driven background head from local withdrawal drawdown, Site-Conditioned Boundary Closure (SCBC) maps local physical descriptors to positive exchange coefficients at the cut boundary. Supervised on unforced donor-domain withdrawal responses, these coefficients yield a passivity-preserving reduced operator that generalizes across unseen forcing histories without refitting. We evaluate SCBC on flood-driven subsurface seepage beneath levee foundations against full-grid reference simulations (MODFLOW~6). Across three held-out foundation panels, a single frozen SCBC tree estimator reduced peak-discharge log RMSE by 26.1%, 30.9% and 42.6% relative to identical local patches using a shared boundary coefficient. We then test whether better screening forecasts improve constrained placement, minimizing peak landside toe head subject to a discharge capacity limit and a budget of three sequential full-grid checks. On a separate 36-foundation test using a coarser 30-state ring operator, a neural SCBC estimator improved discharge forecasts across candidates yet selected four over-capacity placements before checks, compared with one for a shared-coefficient ring, which recovered all 144 reference optima after three checks.

title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
justification: EM fault-injection attacks on model alignment targeting prefill; hardware security, touches inference but not serving optimization.
hype_justification: Striking physical attack with robot-harm demo; famous co-author (Shumailov), likely viral.
abstract: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

title: Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences
justification: Genome-to-image translation, unrelated.
hype_justification: Bioinformatics generation, niche.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate's genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment-contig-isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall.

title: Deneb-Vritra: Descriptions, Edges and Names Examined by Blocking Via Restoring Token Representations and Attention
justification: Interpretability mechanism study of a classification encoder; mentions efficient inference but mechanistic focus.
hype_justification: Dense interpretability study, limited reach.
abstract: Laya is a 421M-parameter encoder that answers a question about a text in one pass: each answer option, written as a name plus a description, gets a marker token, and one score is read from the network at each marker. We first confirm that such models can follow an option's name when it contradicts the description; the question is where in the network this happens. We locate it. On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. Repeated on 5 checkpoints (released, fine-tuned, name-randomised, and a pair trained without two schemas), the knockout finds similar layers; in the name-randomised ones, blocking the description edges instead brings the shortcut back to 56-58%, so the read persists and is outvoted. Marker states decode the name from layer 0; a one-direction probe erasure changed nothing but was weaker than a random edit. Copying layers 0-13 or 14-27 of a name-randomised sibling into a fine-tune recovers 66% and 65% (v1); 21% and 45% (pair A) of its shortcut reduction. 9 of the 12 predictions we could score, written before running, failed. Head sweeps cover 5 of 5 checkpoints; data are synthetic and LLM-labelled; one architecture.

title: Geometry, Reliability, and Spacetime Dynamics of Hyper-Simplex Fractal Networks
justification: P2P network topology/consensus, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Theoretical distributed topology, niche.
abstract: Large-scale, delay-tolerant peer-to-peer networks that need strong consistency usually separate naming, routing, consensus, and ordering into independent layers. To bring deterministic network properties into complex peer-to-peer structures, we unify all four on a single recursive topology. Modeling mutual equality among N peers in Euclidean space requires dimension at least N-1, which prevents flat equal groups from scaling at fixed dimension. The hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m) escapes this limit by recursion. Each non-leaf node anchors a half-scale N-clique. From the resulting digit-word addresses alone, nodes decide adjacency without routing tables, forward greedily along exact shortest paths, and converge geometrically to a self-similar attractor of dimension log_2 N. Running hierarchical PBFT on the same prefix tree achieves linear message load and logarithmic fault-free latency, with an explicit reliability threshold under independent faults and analytical recursions for anchor exposure, dual homing, and event registration. Reversible topology edits generate the Higman-Thompson group V_N on the address boundary, block order characterizes service-topology hosting beyond treewidth, and root-anchored block heights yield persistent spacetime coordinates with compact light-client proofs.

title: Analyzing and Improving FlowMap Distillation of Autoregressive Video Models
justification: FlowMap distillation for autoregressive video generation; inference acceleration but for video diffusion not LLM.
hype_justification: Few-step video generation is hot; strong author team (Jiatao Gu).
abstract: FlowMap distillation offers a natural route to few-step generative modeling by directly learning a teacher's denoising trajectories. Yet for autoregressive (AR) video generation, existing few-step models still rely on distribution matching distillation (DMD) to remain competitive, sacrificing sample diversity and requiring a large bidirectional teacher. In this work, we analyze what limits standalone AR FlowMap distillation and introduce two complementary guidance mechanisms to close this gap: (1) anti-drifting guidance, which helps the AR teacher correct drifted student rollouts by training an auxiliary model to mimic student drift and using it as a negative guidance branch; and (2) motion-aware guidance, which makes motion easier for a FlowMap student to learn by locating motion patches and selectively applying skip-layer guidance. Empirically, our approach applies to $π$-Flow, MeanFlow, and consistency distillation with 1.3B AR teachers, improving generation quality and reducing drift over 30 s rollouts. Notably, our 4-step $π$-Flow students match DMD students distilled from 14B teachers on VBench while preserving the sample diversity of their AR teachers, demonstrating that pure FlowMap distillation is effective for few-step autoregressive video generation.

title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training
justification: Learning-rate transfer across block count in post-training; training-side, not inference.
hype_justification: LR-transfer scaling rules draw some interest; precision angle novel.
abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.

title: Reducing Order Sensitivity in Decision Models
justification: Order-invariance via tree attention for decision models; inference efficiency/robustness angle but specialized decision models.
hype_justification: Weinberger group; tree-attention trick is neat and applicable without retraining.
abstract: Decision models are emerging as fast components of larger AI systems. Yet recent decision models, such as Jev, process options sequentially, leading to different predictions based on their ordering. Across ten open- and closed-source decision models, we find that \emph{order-sensitivity} is pervasive, causing substantial accuracy degradation and unreliable decision-making. These effects become more pronounced as the number of options grows and can compound across multi-step decisions. To address this problem, we systematically compare eight methods for mitigating order sensitivity in terms of robustness, predictive accuracy, and inference efficiency. Among these methods, we find that \emph{tree attention} is a surprisingly effective and efficient method. It achieves order invariance by processing options as parallel branches of a shared context. When used during training, it matches the baseline's average accuracy. Applied to the baseline without retraining, it also eliminates order sensitivity with only a 1.1-point drop in accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that order invariance can be enforced directly in decision models with little or no loss in predictive accuracy.

title: Needwise: Generation-Free Conversational Recommendation from Need-Level Typed Decisions
justification: Generation-free conversational recommender; discusses latency/cost but recommendation-focused.
hype_justification: RecSys efficiency, moderate interest.
abstract: Conversational recommenders must rank items against needs that catalogs record only in part, while users add, withdraw and reverse needs and switch between requests. LLM rankers re-read the dialogue at every turn: they are slow, and their ordering does not show which needs an item meets. We show that a conversational recommender can be built from typed decisions instead: named questions over fixed options, answered with option probabilities rather than generated text. On each turn, one typed request maps the message onto the catalog's fields, keeps what no field expresses in the user's words, and decides how the turn changes each earlier need. Needwise then ranks candidates must-first: the needs on the kind of item, its place and its price form a tier, and within it one holistic decision and need-level verdicts (supported, contradicted or unknown) are combined with equal weight (Needwise-HF). With the graded attributes withheld from the records, so that needs must be inferred from names, descriptions and reviews, Needwise-HF ranks Google Local requests significantly better than GPT-6 Sol (0.383 against 0.343 nDCG@10) and is not significantly different from the strongest LLM ranker on Google Local and Yelp; these comparisons keep their sign under every treatment of unrecorded attributes we test. It costs a fraction of GPT-6 Sol's API price and answers in 2.5 s at the median on Google Local, against 5.6 s for GPT-6 Sol. In conversations, the typed state keeps the ranking across switches and returns, but it recognizes only 19-27% of withdrawn needs.

title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
justification: RL attribution for search agents, not inference systems.
hype_justification: RL interpretability for agents, niche.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.

title: Know When to Abstain: Conformal Confidence Estimation for Text-to-SQL
justification: Conformal confidence for text-to-SQL; abstention not inference serving.
hype_justification: Text-to-SQL reliability, moderate practical interest.
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems often return queries that execute successfully but answer the wrong question. Detecting these errors at deployment is hard because execution correctness is defined against a gold query, which exists only in labeled data. We formulate confidence estimation for Text-to-SQL as probabilistic query validation under a latent correctness variable that is observable at calibration time through gold-SQL execution and latent at deployment. Our estimator separates generation from validation. A generator LLM writes and executes the query, and a different critic LLM judges the query and its execution result. The critic's validation and execution-grounded alignment scores are fused with the generator's verbalized confidence, token-level uncertainty, and SQL-structural features in a Random Forest, using two sequential LLM calls. Two calibration steps give finite-sample guarantees. A Learn-then-Test threshold ensures, with probability $1-δ$, that the error rate among accepted queries stays below a user-chosen budget. A conformal p-value bounds the false abstention rate. On Spider we use GPT-OSS-120B as generator and Gemma-4-31B as critic. The estimator obtains an AUARC of 0.899. Without abstention, 22.6% of queries are wrong. With a 15% risk budget ($δ=0.1$), a threshold is certified on all 10 resampled splits, and the system accepts 52.4% of queries on average with 9.1% observed error. Five different critic models give similar results. In a controlled comparison on Spider with Olmo-3-32B as generator, the estimator obtains an AUARC of 89.5, compared with 81.2 for the strongest logit-based baseline. Applied to BIRD without retraining, the confidence scores remain informative (AUROC 0.72, against 0.79 on Spider), but the risk guarantee does not transfer, as expected without exchangeability.

title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance
justification: Graph RAG for equipment maintenance application, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Deployed Bosch production RAG system adds credibility, some interest.
abstract: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.

title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
justification: Verifying PDE solver outputs, unrelated.
hype_justification: Numerical verification, niche.
abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
justification: VLM active spatial exploration benchmark, not inference.
hype_justification: Spatial reasoning benchmark, moderate.
abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

title: Agentic AI for Intent Management and Control in Autonomous Communication Networks
justification: Agentic AI for network intent management, unrelated.
hype_justification: Telecom agentic AI, niche.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation will help future mobile networks translate high-level network intents into concrete network optimization or control actions. However, existing approaches often focus on intent management and orchestration, leaving the adaptation of underlying network optimization and control functions largely unaddressed. This article proposes a triadic agentic AI framework that co-designs intent management and intent fulfillment through three agents: an interpreter, powered by a language model, that translates and refines intents into machine-readable optimization templates; an optimizer that adapts controller policies to intent specifications; and a controller that performs fast decision-making. We discuss the design space of each agent and how the workflow can be embedded across network architectural domains. Finally, we develop a concrete realization combining a language-model interpreter with Bayesian optimization for the optimizer and multi-objective reinforcement learning for the controller, and evaluate it in a radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity. Results demonstrate how the agentic AI framework can connect high-level intents with runtime network control, showing adaptability of intent specifications and control policies to service requirements and changing network conditions.

title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
justification: LLM self-monitoring/uncertainty study, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Self-correction limitations topical; single author.
abstract: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

title: TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
justification: CLIP dual-encoder modality gap correction, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Training-free CLIP retrieval fix, broad applicability to embeddings.
abstract: CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test. We introduce a paired statistic that identifies directions where the two towers agree more on hard negatives than on matched pairs. Mildly attenuating these directions improves retrieval while largely preserving the gap. We arrive at this correction through weight-space programming: guided by the statistic, an LLM agent inspects both towers and writes closed-form weight edits without backpropagation. Free to edit any component, the agent improves COCO test retrieval on all 13 CLIP checkpoints and edits an output projection in 12 of the 13. We distill and refine its recurring correction into TowerBridge, a closed-form recipe motivated by a first-order analysis of the hard-negative margin. Computed in seconds from 25,000 labelled pairs, it requires no model-specific tuning and leaves the architecture and inference cost unchanged. TowerBridge improves COCO test retrieval by 16.8 RSUM and Flickr30k test retrieval by 6.6 on average across all 21 evaluated CLIP checkpoints, including 8 unseen by the agent, while limiting any drop in ImageNet zero-shot accuracy to 0.5 points. It also reduces hubness on all 21 checkpoints and improves retrieval on 4 of 5 dual encoders from other families.

title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
justification: Unified multimodal generation from VLM representations, not inference serving.
hype_justification: Unified understanding+generation is trending.
abstract: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.

title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
justification: Structured pruning of driving VLAs for inference speedup and lower memory; clear inference-optimization relevance.
hype_justification: NVIDIA Alpamayo-based, pruning for deployment; practical and adoptable.
abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.

title: Solving Attention Kernel Regression Problem via Pre-conditioner
justification: Fast algorithms for attention-matrix proxy regression via sketching; attention efficiency theory, tangential to serving.
hype_justification: Theoretical attention algorithms; Zhao Song group, limited practical uptake.
abstract: The attention mechanism is the key to large language models, and the attention matrix serves as an algorithmic and computational bottleneck for such a scheme. In this paper, we define two problems, motivated by designing fast algorithms for proxy of attention matrix and solving regressions against them. Given an input matrix $A\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and a response vector $b$, the first proxy, for $n\gg d$, uses powers of the matrix $A^\top A$, and we consider two types of regression problems: $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}\|(A^\top A)^jx-b\|_2$ and $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^d}\|A(A^\top A)^jx-b\|_2$ for any positive integer $j$. We design fast algorithms for these power regressions, based on sketching and preconditioning. The second proxy is applying exponential entrywise to the Gram matrix, denoted by $\exp(AA^\top)$ and solving the regression $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^n}\|\exp(AA^\top)x-b \|_2$. We call this problem the attention kernel regression problem, as the matrix $\exp(AA^\top)$ could be viewed as a kernel function with respect to $A$. For this problem, we show that the sketching and preconditioning approach known for Gaussian kernels gives error $ε\|b\|_2$ for every $b$, with a sketch dimension that is, up to logarithmic factors, $ε^{-2}n$ times the condition number of the kernel matrix, which is at least $n/e$ when the rows of $A$ have norm at most $1$. For rows of norm at most $1$, we also give an algorithm whose sketch dimension, up to logarithmic factors, does not depend on $n$. It sketches the kernel plus a ridge term, and for a given $K\geq 1$ its error is at most $ε\|b\|_2$ plus $(1+\sqrtε)$ times the best residual among solutions of norm at most $(K/n)\|b\|_2$. We hope these efforts will provide an alternative perspective of studying efficient approximation of attention matrices.

title: Feriji: A French-Zarma Parallel Corpus, Glossary & Translator
justification: French-Zarma translation corpus, unrelated.
hype_justification: Low-resource MT, niche but socially valued.
abstract: Machine translation (MT) is a rapidly expanding field that has experienced significant advancements in recent years with the development of models capable of translating multiple languages with remarkable accuracy. However, the representation of African languages in this field still needs to improve due to linguistic complexities and limited resources. This applies to the Zarma language, a dialect of Songhay (of the Nilo-Saharan language family) spoken by over 5 million people across Niger and neighboring countries \cite{lewis2016ethnologue}. This paper introduces Feriji, the first robust French-Zarma parallel corpus and glossary designed for MT. The corpus, containing 61,085 sentences in Zarma and 42,789 in French, and a glossary of 4,062 words represent a significant step in addressing the need for more resources for Zarma. We fine-tune three large language models on our dataset, obtaining a BLEU score of 30.06 on the best-performing model. We further evaluate the models on human judgments of fluency, comprehension, and readability and the importance and impact of the corpus and models. Our contributions help to bridge a significant language gap and promote an essential and overlooked indigenous African language.

title: Grammatical Error Correction for Low-Resource Languages: The Case of Zarma
justification: Grammatical error correction for Zarma, unrelated.
hype_justification: Low-resource NLP, niche.
abstract: Grammatical error correction (GEC) aims to improve text quality and readability. Previous work on the task focused primarily on high-resource languages, while low-resource languages lack robust tools. To address this shortcoming, we present a study on GEC for Zarma, a language spoken by over five million people in West Africa. We compare three approaches: rule-based methods, machine translation (MT) models, and large language models (LLMs). We evaluated GEC models using a dataset of more than 250,000 examples, including synthetic and human-annotated data. Our results showed that the MT-based approach using M2M100 outperforms others, with a detection rate of 95.82% and a suggestion accuracy of 78.90% in automatic evaluations (AE) and an average score of 3.0 out of 5.0 in manual evaluation (ME) from native speakers for grammar and logical corrections. The rule-based method was effective for spelling errors but failed on complex context-level errors. LLMs -- Gemma 2b and MT5-small -- showed moderate performance. Our work supports use of MT models to enhance GEC in low-resource settings, and we validated these results with Bambara, another West African language.

title: On the Efficiency of Structured Pruning in Small Language Model Pretraining
justification: Structured pruning for small LM pretraining; compression but training-cost focused, not inference serving.
hype_justification: Apple authors, enlarge-and-prune is practically relevant for edge deployment.
abstract: Companies that deploy generative language models on edge devices often need to train small models from scratch due to legal, data-governance, or product-customization requirements. An alternative approach is to train an enlarged model and compress it to the target size via structured pruning, but this advantage becomes unclear once the cost of pretraining the enlarged model is included. We introduce the enlarge-and-prune framework to study this question under full-cost accounting, and show that conventional enlarge-and-prune pipelines -- which train the enlarged model, prune it, and recover in separate stages -- do not consistently outperform direct small-model training under the same total token budget. To overcome this limitation, we propose IDEA Prune, an integrated enlarge-and-prune pipeline that unifies enlarged model pretraining, iterative structured pruning, and recovery under a single cosine annealing learning rate schedule. In controlled experiments compressing 2.8B models to 1.3B with up to 2T tokens on the same dataset, IDEA Prune consistently outperforms conventional pipelines and modestly improves overall performance relative to the scratch baseline, improving MMLU accuracy to 46.4%, compared with 31.4-33.4% for conventional pipelines. These advantages are preserved after downstream supervised fine-tuning, where IDEA Prune matches or outperforms all baselines of the same size on instruction following, math reasoning, and code generation. Our analysis further reveals that intermediate checkpoints provide more favorable pruning starting points than fully converged ones, and that an enlargement factor of approximately 2.6x yields the best pruned models in the tested regime.

title: Virology Capabilities Test (VCT): A Multimodal Virology Q&A Benchmark
justification: Virology Q&A benchmark, unrelated.
hype_justification: Dual-use biosecurity + Hendrycks; governance angle draws attention.
abstract: We present the Virology Capabilities Test (VCT), a large language model (LLM) benchmark that measures the capability to troubleshoot complex virology laboratory protocols. Constructed from the inputs of dozens of PhD-level expert virologists, VCT consists of $322$ multimodal questions covering fundamental, tacit, and visual knowledge that is essential for practical work in virology laboratories. VCT is difficult: expert virologists with access to the internet score an average of $22.1\%$ on questions specifically in their sub-areas of expertise. However, the most performant LLM, OpenAI's o3, reaches $43.8\%$ accuracy, outperforming $94\%$ of expert virologists even within their sub-areas of specialization. The ability to provide expert-level virology troubleshooting is inherently dual-use: it is useful for beneficial research, but it can also be misused. Therefore, the fact that publicly available models outperform virologists on VCT raises pressing governance considerations. We propose that the capability of LLMs to provide expert-level troubleshooting of dual-use virology work should be integrated into existing frameworks for handling dual-use technologies in the life sciences.

title: Fortune: Formula-Driven Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning over Complex Tables
justification: RL for table reasoning via formulas, unrelated to inference.
hype_justification: Microsoft authors, table reasoning RL moderate interest.
abstract: Tables are a fundamental medium for organizing and analyzing data, making table reasoning an essential capability for intelligent systems. Although large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong general reasoning abilities, they still struggle with accurate numerical reasoning over tabular data, particularly in complex table settings that require more than simple relational lookup. Spreadsheet formulas provide a powerful and expressive interface for executable symbolic operations, enabling sophisticated reasoning patterns that remain largely underexplored by existing LLMs. In this paper, we introduce Formula Tuning (Fortune), a formula-driven reinforcement learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to generate executable spreadsheet formulas for question answering over tabular data, using execution success and answer correctness as reward signals. Building upon Fortune, we train Formula-R1 and evaluate its performance across seven table reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating competitive performance, particularly on tasks involving complex tables and multi-step numerical computation. Furthermore, Formula-R1-Plus, which integrates textual and formula-based reasoning, achieves further performance improvements. Beyond these empirical results, we provide insights into the roles of reinforcement learning and executable formula representations in table reasoning, highlighting the broader potential of symbolic RL to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

title: Text-to-Image Prompt Optimization for Unseen Rewards
justification: Text-to-image prompt optimization, unrelated.
hype_justification: T2I prompt optimization, moderate.
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) prompt optimization rewrites user prompts to improve the quality of generated images under a target reward. Existing methods typically assume a known reward, relying on reward-specific training or handcrafted instructions. We instead study prompt optimization for unseen rewards, which are unknown at design time and accessible only through scores at test time. We observe that removing reward-specific guidance substantially reduces the search efficiency of LLM-based optimizers, even though their optimization histories contain evidence of what the reward favors. To address this challenge, we introduce RATTPO (Reward-Adaptive Test-Time Prompt Optimization), a reward-generic method that turns this implicit evidence into explicit search guidance. At each round, RATTPO contrasts high- and low-scoring prompts to infer competing hypotheses about promising rewriting directions, then generates and evaluates candidates under each hypothesis. Across four reward families, RATTPO consistently outperforms reward-generic baselines at equal budgets and achieves performance comparable to reward-tailored optimizers without any reward-specific adjustment.

title: Reducing Pipeline Bubbles in Message-Efficient State Machine Replication
justification: State machine replication pipelining; distributed systems but not LLM inference.
hype_justification: RDMA SMR with strong throughput; systems-conference interest, not LLM.
abstract: Round-based pipelining in state machine replication (SMR) protocols reduces amortized bottleneck message complexity to $O(1)$, but waiting for network propagation and accommodating timing variation create pipeline bubbles that can erase this benefit. We present Chora, a message-efficient SMR protocol co-designed with a network runtime to minimize these bubbles under common-case synchrony. Chora introduces a new round construct that decouples propagation delay from round length. It then builds a carefully engineered runtime that minimizes variation in processing jitter. The co-designed protocol leverages strong synchrony to achieve $O(1)$ amortized bottleneck message complexity with high resource utilization, and maintains safety and liveness when timing predictability degrades. Evaluation shows that Chora reaches 3.92 million operations per second with five RDMA replicas, achieving 2.87$\times$ throughput of the state-of-the-art, while maintaining comparable latency. Even on this single-hop RDMA network that favors conventional rounds, Chora reduces time lost to pipeline bubbles, leaving more CPU time for protocol processing. Across three to seven replicas, the CPU utilization rate for protocol processing increases by 211%--421% and throughput improves by 5.3--6.6$\times$ over conventional rounds.

title: EEG-MedRAG: Enhancing EEG-based Clinical Decision-Making via Hierarchical Hypergraph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
justification: EEG clinical RAG system, unrelated.
hype_justification: Medical hypergraph RAG, niche.
abstract: With the widespread application of electroencephalography (EEG) in neuroscience and clinical practice, efficiently retrieving and semantically interpreting large-scale, multi-source, heterogeneous EEG data has become a pressing challenge. EEG-MedRAG addresses this challenge through a three-layer hypergraph-based retrieval-augmented generation framework that unifies EEG domain knowledge, individual patient cases, and large-scale EEG recordings into a traversable n-ary relational hypergraph, enabling joint semantic-temporal retrieval and evidence-grounded clinical reasoning. The accompanying benchmark is the first to pair EEG questions about the same clinical fact across five user roles. Its 700 questions span seven clinical domains and support direct comparisons of answer consistency across roles. Across three LLM backbones, EEG-MedRAG outperforms all four baselines in both overall answer correctness and token-level F1. It achieves up to 86.14% answer correctness on the full benchmark and 97.32% on non-EEG questions, with 97.41% evidence coverage on knowledge questions. In EEG retrieval, EEG-MedRAG improves top-five label agreement by 8.58 percentage points over the time-series baseline. The code is available at https://github.com/li-zan/EEG-MedRAG.

title: Playing Markov Games Without Observing Payoffs
justification: Markov games without payoffs, theory, unrelated.
hype_justification: Online learning theory, niche.
abstract: Optimization under uncertainty is a fundamental problem in learning and decision-making, particularly in multi-agent systems. Previously, Feldman, Kalai, and Tennenholtz [2010] demonstrated the ability to efficiently compete in repeated symmetric two-player matrix games without observing payoffs, as long as the opponents actions are observed. In this paper, we introduce and formalize a new class of zero-sum symmetric Markov games, which extends the notion of symmetry from matrix games to the Markovian setting. We show that even without observing payoffs, a player who knows the transition dynamics and observes only the opponents sequence of actions can still compete against an adversary who may have complete knowledge of the game. We formalize three distinct notions of symmetry in this setting and show that, under these conditions, the learning problem can be reduced to an instance of online learning, enabling the player to asymptotically match the return of the opponent despite lacking payoff observations. Our algorithms apply to both matrix and Markov games, and run in polynomial time with respect to the size of the game and the number of episodes. Our work broadens the class of games in which robust learning is possible under severe informational disadvantage and deepens the connection between online learning and adversarial game theory.

title: Patient-Zero: Scaling Synthetic Patient Agents to Real-World Distributions without Real Patient Data
justification: Synthetic patient agents, unrelated.
hype_justification: Synthetic medical data, moderate.
abstract: Synthetic data generation with Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising solution in the medical domain to mitigate data scarcity and privacy constraints. However, existing approaches remain constrained by their derivative nature, relying on real-world records, which pose privacy risks and distribution biases. Furthermore, current patient agents face the Stability-Plasticity Dilemma, struggling to maintain clinical consistency during dynamic inquiries. To address these challenges, we introduce Patient-Zero, a novel framework for ab initio patient simulation that requires no real medical records. Our Medically-Aligned Hierarchical Synthesis framework generates comprehensive and diverse patient records from medical knowledge via stratified attribute permutation. To support rigorous clinical interaction, we design a Dual-Track Cognitive Memory System to enable agents dynamically update memory while preserving logical consistency and persona adherence. Extensive evaluations show that Patient-Zero outperforms baselines in both data quality and interaction fidelity. In physician evaluations, our records obtain the highest mean diversity, consistency, and completeness ratings. Downstream medical reasoning model trained on our synthetic dataset shows substantial performance gains (MedQA +24.0%; MMLU +14.5%), demonstrating the practical utility of our framework.

title: Rethinking Multiplication in Neural Networks with Hadamard Transform-Assisted Operators
justification: Multiplication-avoiding Hadamard operators for compute-in-memory inference; inference-efficiency but CNN/CIM not LLM.
hype_justification: CIM efficiency niche, incremental on CNNs.
abstract: Multiplication-avoiding neural operators are attractive for compute-in-memory (CIM) architectures, but directly replacing conventional convolutions often causes accuracy degradation. We investigate whether this limitation arises from multiplication avoidance itself or from the representation on which the operator acts. In this work, we introduce Hadamard Transform-assisted multiplication-avoiding (HMA) operators that combine Walsh--Hadamard transform features with multiplication-avoiding channel mixing. To identify where conventional multiplication remains necessary, we employ a gated formulation in which conventional and HMA operators compete through learned layer-wise coefficients. ResNet-18 experiments show that intermediate convolutional layers assign greater weight to HMA, whereas the earliest layers and final classifier retain greater contribution from conventional computation. Guided by this observation, we construct a compact hybrid HMA network and train it using knowledge distillation from a conventional teacher. On CIFAR-10, the resulting ResNet-18 student achieves 91.2\% accuracy compared with 90.4\% for the corresponding conventional baseline while reducing parameters by 68.25\%, conventional MACs by 85.71\%, and general multiplications by 85.54\%. Across ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and MobileNetV2 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, HMA with knowledge distillation matches or improves the conventional models. These results show that Hadamard-domain feature restructuring can improve the accuracy--complexity tradeoff of multiplication-avoiding networks and provide a practical path toward efficient CIM inference.

title: Binding Constraints in a Strategic Technology: An Industrial Vulnerability Index for the Foundation Model Industry
justification: AI industry vulnerability index (compute/energy economics), not inference systems.
hype_justification: AI compute/energy policy angle topical.
abstract: Industrial policy directed at artificial intelligence has become substantial. Public investment concentrates on compute, where private capacity expansion is already underway, and is largely absent from grid interconnection and generation. Whether that allocation accurately reflects the most binding constraint in production has not yet been systematically measured.
